THE SMITHSONIAN INSTITUTION

Jazz Oral History Project
Interview with Jay McShann
Sides 1-2
Conducted by Stanley and Helen Dance.
December 11, 1978

PRO-TYPISTS, INC.
PROFESSIONAL TRANSCRIPTION SERVICE
AREA CODE 202 347-5395
PROCEEDINGS
This is an interview with Jay McShann on December the 11th, 1978, for the Smithsonian Institution. Well, Jay, when were you born and where?
I was born in Muskogee, Oklahoma, on January the 12th, 1916.
19 when?
16, I'm sorry.
(Laughter.)
I thought you said 60.
(Laughter.)
Yes. Well, and in our family there was four kids and Dad and mother.
Were they boys or girls?
Three elder girls and myself. I was the youngest.
You were the only boy.
Yes.
Oh, were you spoiled?
Oh, I don't think so because -- well, you know, you take three girls and a mother in a home, there's no chance for -- even being the youngest boy, to get spoiled
because, you know, you can't win.
(Laughter.)
You were outnumbered.
I was outnumbered.
And were your parents musical at all?
Well, the only thing that I did notice, my mother, she played a few church songs.
On piano?

On piano, you know, and my dad, he only did one tune and that was the only thing I ever heard him do and I never did know what that tune was called, but it was just -- you know, like you see people hanging around with the piano player, little "Boiling Cabbage," something like that, and as far as I can remember, there was one of those little type tunes like "Boiling Cabbage" or something like that.
(Laughter.)
Were your sisters musical at all?
Well, no, they weren't, because -- well, you know, we were a very poor family and --
What did your father do?

Well, my daddy, he drove a truck. He was a truckdriver, and worked at a furniture store and used to do long-distance hauling and you know, did other things in the furniture store, like laying linoleum and laying rugs and you
know, the stoves, put stoves up and things like that, you know and then a lot of times, he'd have to make long trips to deliver furniture, maybe two, three, 400, 500 miles, like that.
That was a long way in those days.

Oh, it was. That was a long ways, because a lot of times, I would always beg him to take me with him, you know, and he did on a couple of occasions, but my mother, she didn't go for it too well, you know? She soon shut that out.
Was he working for one company all that time?
Well, he worked for one company, I think, about 25 or 27 years. That was Ferguson Brothers Furniture Company.
Was this in Muskogee?
This was in Muskogee.
Where is Muskogee?
Muskogee was about 30,000 population and even today, I don't think it's too much over 30. It might be 40, you know, after all these years has passed. It might be 40 or close to 40.
And what goes on there? What made Muskogee? Was it a railroad junction or something?
Well, not, it wasn't railroad junction, although they had about -- of course, during those days, you
know, they had two or three railroads running in there, you know, like -- oh, let's see. I imagine the Midland Valley, the Frisco and Katy -- K&T --
How far from Kansas City is it?
Well, I would say it's close to about 275 or 80 miles and probably during that time, it was about 300 miles from Kansas City.
What's the biggest city nearest to Muskogee?
Well, the biggest city nearest to Muskogee would be Tulsa, Oklahoma, which was about 60 miles from Muskogee.
What about your grandparents? I mean, who first came to Muskogee?
Well, I think my grandmother on my mother's side was the first to come to Muskogee.
From where?

And she came from Texas, originally from Alabama, then Texas and then to Oklahoma. Well, you know, during those days, you know, during the -- it was called Indian Territory then -- and everybody was talking about going to Indian Territory. So that's why I think that she came there with the intentions of signing up for -- I forget how much land, you know, they would allow you to sign up for.
Yeah, that was when the land was thrown
Yes, you know.
Was there Indian blood in your family on your grandmother's side or no? Or --

Well, to tell you the truth, I don't think so, I don't think so. No, I don't think there was any Indian blood. But you see, there was so many colored people that looked like Indians, you know, so many of us that looked like Indians, so many, and so they just sign up as an Indian, sign up for the land. But unfortunately, she -- oh, I heard my mother talk about it and something that happened. She had to go back to Texas. She went back to Texas for, I think it was for a matter of a few days. When she came back, the period was over with. So that's how she missed out on that.

Because they -- I can remember my mother telling me, they was trying to get her to hurry at the time that they got there, to hurry up and sign up for it. She had something that she wanted to do and so we missed that.
Then on my father's side, they were from Mississippi, the McShanns, they were from Mississippi, and they came and settled in Texas and he met my mother after leaving Texas, coming to Oklahoma.
What was your mother's name?
Her name was Leona McBee
McBee?
Uh-huh.
B-double E?
Uh-huh.
Well, you have some Scottish blood in there too, haven't you?
(Laughter.)
Both sides.
Yeah.

You know, I was talking to Duke Ellington's sister and she said there was Indian blood on his father's side. (Inaudible). But there's a lot of -- I think (inaudible) -- you know, there were so many people like Jimmy Blanton and Oscar Pettiford -- they were all supposed to have it.

Well, Oscar Pettiford, from what I understand, the Pettiford family, they had Indian blood. Now, they were from, if I make no mistake, I think it was Okmulgee, Oklahoma, and that's only about 30 miles from Muskogee.

Well, the reason we are interested in it, it seems possible that even in this music, there is an Indian contribution that has never really been -- you know, they talk of the racial thing and how it affects the nature of the music and it seems possible that there is an Indian thing in there, too, that has never been recognized, you know?
Well, I'm sure there is, because

being from Oklahoma, I was exposed to a lot of Indians, and Indians, you know what I mean, you got a chance to see a lot of things, how they did things this way or that way or the other, you know. And in fact, even later years, after I was even trying to play music, you know, I was way up in the northern part of Oklahoma around Ponca City, they've got a lot of those Ponca Indians up there and four or five different tribes, you know, and they used to come in there with the big cowboy boots and hats on and there was a club they used to come in and in fact, everybody used to go there -- white, Indians, black, everybody. You know, they'd get rough in this club, you know.

There was a colored fella that ran this club. They called him Alligator, you know, and he was kind of a rough-looking guy, you know. I guess because he looked like an alligator, you know. I guess that's the reason they called him.
(Laughter.)

And so, you know, he was kind of rough-looking and I mean, they'd get in there and Alligator would be gone and they'd start fighting and carrying on and somebody would say, 'Go get Alligator.' Alligator would come in there and clean the house completely out. Everybody would go back to their business, if they were shooting the dice or whatever they were doing or if they were drinking the booze or whatever they were

doing. Everything quiet down. "Oh-oh, here comes Alligator." And everything would stop. He was a rough customer, you know, and I'd hate to see Alligator leave because I was in my teens and around there trying to play and I hate to see Alligator leave because they could get pretty rough. They'd come in and put their .45s on the table like that, you know.
(Inaudible).
Yes.
(Laughter.)
But is that true in your experience that Indians didn't take liquor very well? I mean, do you think they got disorderly quicker than others?
Well, I'll tell you what I really think. I've seen a lot of Indians that drink and that could drink and I've seen Indians that couldn't drink.
(Inaudible)?

I've seen Indians that could drink and Indians that couldn't drink. You see, because I think it's the person. Having been around so many of them, you know what I mean. But I think it's really the person because I've seen friends of mine that could drink and friends that couldn't drink and if they got so much in them, they just went the other way, you know? So consequently, then, too, I think Indians felt -- it wasn't hard for them to go haywire. I think due to the way the situation and everything was and had been, you know.
Yeah, yeah.
And when a guy's got things on his mind like that, it creates a different story, complete different atmosphere.
Narrow horizons that they had.

That's right. And -- because I have seen some that take it. I mean, they sit there and drink and never change, you know what I mean. But they often seem to think -- you know, you read a lot about -- they say, "Well, when he'd get that firewater in him, he would go crazy," you know. But he didn't go crazier than anybody else, you know, that couldn't handle it. He didn't go any crazier. You know, that's the way I see it.

But that's the truth. It's the same with any people. I mean, some people really haven't got the stomach for liquor. Some people don't eat right. And then some people makes them mean and evil and other people, it makes them jolly and foolish.
(Laughter.)
Yes.
Indians, the same.
Jay, Lowell Folsom came from a reservation in Oklahoma. Did you know him?
Yes, I know Lowell. Lowell, he's one of those Okies. Yes. And he can sing the blues, too. Yes, he does a good job of the blues, you know, and of course,

as you say, I think there's been a lot of guys that -- musicians even that are -- you know, mix with Indians in Texas, out of Oklahoma, you know what I mean. But then too, you see, there was a lot of people that wouldn't dare say what they were, you know what I mean. They hid behind the curtain for a long time. There was a whole lot of people. A lot of people changed their names, you know what I mean?
Like Fosse, you mean?
How's that?
Posse, you mean?

Well, even that, even that. But a lot of people didn't want them to know -- some of them, if they could pass, they didn't want them to know -- want anybody to know they had Indian blood because they figured it would hurt them. You take a real light colored person, a real light -- I've seen a lot of them -- they had -- could pass, and they could pass, they didn't want nobody to know.
That would be -- I mean, wasn't Jack Teagarden and Mildred Bailey, they were both supposed to have been part Indian, weren't they?
That's true, yes, yes. That's true. And this other girl that sang the blues -- I'm trying to think of what her name was. Of course, she admitted hers.
Well, Mildred admitted hers, too.
Yes, yes. There's a lot of them that
didn't mind. They just come right on out.
But different periods of history, where they would think it would be bad for getting jobs or something like that. Do you think --

Well, a lot of times that happened, you know, people didn't want to -- I know a fella that -- one of the first fellas when I was in school. His name was Dizzy Green, and Orville Green was his real name and his folks just looked like they were white, you know, and he looked white, see? But for some reason, they were colored, you know? And so he and I -- he used to fool around on the guitar and I'd fool around on the piano, you know what I mean, and so he left Muskogee and went to the coast, West Coast, because he wanted to better himself, I'm sure. So after he went to the West Coast, then I ran into a bunch of fellows that used to hang around us all the time and the first thing when I got to California, they told me, they says, 'Man, if you see Orville Green, don't say anything to him, man, because the cat going to sure make you feel bad.' I says, 'What do you mean?' And so this guy told me, he says, 'Well, man, you see, when I was out there in Hollywood,' he says, 'and I happened to look, see four or five guys talking, and I recognized Orville Green. I ran over there and says, 'Hi there, Orville. How you doing, man?' So Orville says, 'Well, hello there. Listen here, I'll tell you what you do. I'm real
busy right now. But come on by the house. I'm sure my mother or aunt will have some work for you to do. Come on by there any time."
(Laughter.)

And this guy really got angry at Orville. He got angry because he said, "Look, that guy had the nerve to pull that on me," you know? But you see, Orville had something else in mind. He had one thing in mind and he felt like that he didn't want to hurt his chances out there in Hollywood because this guy's knowing him because they say, "Hey, man, who's that? What do you know about this guy?" You know what I mean. And so consequently he set it all in front right away.
(Laughter.)
And passed the word along.
(Laughter.)
But you know, the opposite of that was Willie Smith with Lunceford.
Yes. There you go.
I mean, he looked as white as anybody.
Willie could have passed anytime he got ready, but he never did.
Well, it's stupid really, any way you look at it.
Well, Earl Warren. In fact, Earl
Warren, he could really tell you some good stories. I know he's told you some.
: When he was in the South and they all had to stay in terrible places. He'd walk into a good hotel and make them mad.
(Laughter.)

And then a lot of times, he'd probably have to go get food for them. You know? And it's funny, but it's true. I had a white fella that was playing with me. We were down South one time. And I think it was going through either Georgia or Alabama and we stopped to get gas and that's when they had colored restrooms and they had white restrooms. So, you know, quite naturally, him being with the band, you know, he -- we stopped to pull in there and he just went on to the restroom. Well, it was this white restroom. Well, he come out. The fella happened to see him come out. He didn't know that he went in there, the filling station attendant, and he come back, say, "Say, boy don't you know that's a white restroom?" So I winked at the -- he was a trumpet player -- I winked at him, so then he says, "No, I'm sorry. I thought that was the restroom and I just went to the restroom and I didn't think." He says, "Let me get you straight right now." And he went around and showed him where the colored restroom was and the guy was just as white. He was white, you know, and I just kept winking at him until -- you know. Then he

told him he was sorry and then the guy got so mad at the station, he wanted to fight him, you know. So I says, "Oh no, everything's all right. I'll get him out of here. I'll take care of him." So we got on out of there, you know. And it was just something like that and the guy was white, but he figured that he had to be colored because he was with us.
And he probably would have made trouble if he'd known he was anyway.
Well, that's true. You know what I mean.
Yes.
So, it's like you say, six and a half a dozen.

I was in South America with Duke and they were loading the plane up, half of it with melons and half with people. So the band -- he had a white bass player. His instrument had gone through with all the others. So now they've got to load Duke Ellington's band on. They all went on the plane. They wouldn't let the bass player and me through because we were white and they thought, "You don't belong with them." We had a big argument before we could get on the plane.
(Laughter.)
They wouldn't let Ellington's band through?
They let Duke through. They wouldn't let (inaudible).

They let Duke -- they knew the band, you see, so there was the bass player and I. We come up to go and they wouldn't let us through and we couldn't talk any Portuguese. Eventually Paul Gonsalves came up and explained the whole thing.
How about that.
(Laughter.)

Well, you know, you find all these different laws and things and I think why you ran into so much of that, people were making laws for their own conveniences during those times, you know, and the people thought -- didn't think big -- the people, I think, and it shows the way they thought small, you know what I mean?
That was a hangover from slavery.
Yes.
I mean, it was a matter of keeping the people down. That's really what it was, wasn't it?
Right.
You know, and they'd do it as long as they could get away with it.
That's true.
Well, let's go back to the --
The family.
To Muskogee and the family. Well, we talked about your father and mother and your sisters, but
now when do you start to get -- you know, when does music start to enter your life?

Well, I'll tell you, I really -- I used to go to take my sisters, you know, go along with them when they would take their lesson. My mother gave them lessons. The family was poor and so she would try to give the girls lessons. Well, the two older girls, they didn't care anything about it at all and then the next girl, she took some interest in it, you know, no more than just your --
Enough to --
Read, you know, and she did better than the other two. The other two, they didn't care anything about it and didn't try to do anything and --
Did you have a piano in the house then?

We did have a piano in the house and the first thing that ever made me think about any music was the fact that we had a old graphophone -- we called them graphophone in those days -- with the old bulldog up there sitting up there and this horn went out, you know?
(Laughter.)

So sometimes my dad would bring records from the furniture store and he didn't know what he was bringing. So, you know what I mean. If he brought Blue Heaven, he thought that was great because he liked Blue Heaven, see? Or if he
brought some church songs, that was great, you know? But one day, he brought a Mamie Smith or a Bessie Smith record --
(Laughter)
-- and he put it on and I liked it, you know, but he says, "We're going to get rid of that record."
Were your mother and father sort of church-going people?

They were church-going people. Both church-going. And they would frown upon those kind of records, you know, but I'd always make it my business to try to hide the records and before they could get rid of them, I'd hide them somewhere. I'd get rid of the records for them, you know, and so, you know, when I was in school -- you know when you're in school, there's always a music teacher that comes around, you know, and I had never given any thought to music one way or the other and there was a teacher named Elsie Clark -- well, I'm sure she was up in age, but she would come around and that's when they had you singing from -- you know, you just sing, they would teach you the songs orally, you know.
Just say her name again, will you, Jay?

This was Elsie Clark. And she -- the way she would do, she would go to all the schools, but we only got that music maybe once every two or three weeks, you know. But I was always glad to see her come in and I never knew why,
but it seemed like it always felt good when Miss Clark would come in. They'd say, "Oh, Miss Clark will be here today," you know.
But anyway, later on, --
She would be teaching or just singing?
Yeah, just singing.
Would she be -- what would she have taught you? Would she have taught you the value of the notes or --
No.
No?
No, just singing, just orally, just singing, you know.
Yeah.

Because I think the piano that she had, it was just about gone, too, you know, but she could get by and she'd get her point across, you know, and so I never really had given music any thought but later on, after I got further along in school, I -- they had a band instructor -- they finally got a band instructor there and so they was trying to get parents to buy the instruments for their kids, you know. Well, my parents couldn't afford no instrument for me and so they just told the instructor, says, "No, we cannot afford no instrument," because they didn't want me to have any kind of

horn. It didn't make any difference, you know. And so that knocked me out there and back to when my mother was sending me to lessons with my sister, I got so sick and tired of listening to my sister make mistakes and I went up there and played it for her. I said, "This is the way this goes," and I played it for my sister and the teacher was in the back room, you know, she had some beans on, cooking beans. She went to see about her beans. So she hollered, "Now, that's the way I've been trying to get you to do that all the time." She come back in there and she said, "Now, do that again." Sister said "I didn't do it," she says, "he did."
(Laughter.)

Her name was Mrs. Aires. So she looked at me, she says, "You did that?" I said, "Yes." She said, "All right, do it again." So I did. So she said, "Okay." She sent my mother a note. She says, "Don't send this boy with these girls to take their music lessons anymore, because he's getting a lesson free."
(Laughter.)
So, well, you know what I mean.
That was her reaction.

But she did in the meantime finally told my mother, she says, "I'll tell you what." She said, "You're spending your money foolishly. The girls don't care anything about it. I'm going to tell you. Give that boy lessons."

But you know, my mother, you know how some people feel, she says, "Oh, this boy will never use it. He'll never do this. He'll never do that." And she says, "Well --" "And we don't have the money." So she just, you know -- so finally, I would sneak up to the piano and start picking out things, you know, start picking out little things on the piano.
Like how old would you be here, ten?
I'd say about ten, 11, you know, start picking out a few little things, and then --
By ear?
Uh-huh.
Not from notes — you couldn't read.

Something you heard. And then in the meantime, you'd be playing these records, you know, playing the records and things like that. And so now I'm getting on up there about 13 or 14 years old, you see, so by 13, 14, this fellow that took over the music department in the school, he came in the room one day and I was sitting down playing and he heard me playing and he says, "Look, I want you to play at the --" What was that they used to have? You know, they'd have, where everybody would go to the auditorium?
Commencement?
It wasn't commencement. They used to call it --
Oh, Convocation or something?
Yeah, where everybody goes to the auditorium and maybe the principal -- they used to call it sort of a pep meeting, you know.
When you all went there in the morning, do you mean?
No, like all the classes would come to the auditorium and --
Not everyday or --

Not everyday, no. Maybe this was just once every two weeks or something like that and like they would have a little pep meeting or something, they would call it. The principal might talk about something or somebody else talk about something and then they might have somebody to sing something. But he wanted me to play. And I says, "I can't play. I don't play. I can't play up there." So he says, "Just do what you did," and I didn't want to and I begged out of it. But I'll tell you what happened.

He called on me anyhow. So he called on me anyhow. So I went on up and the only thing that I knew was that thing that I had heart Bessie Smith do, you know, which was backwater blues, you know? And I just started playing that and the kids in school screamed and you know how they do and clapped their hands and screamed. And the next day in school, I caught it from everybody. The teacher was talking about me in my class. She says, "I think it was a shame a member of our class got up

there and played what he played," and the principal, everybody. "I'll never play anything." So I said -- so I didn't fool with no music. You know, I felt so bad. So I wouldn't play at the school no more. They come back and try to get me to play, you know?
I take it that these sort of church and sort of school people thought blues was too lowdown or something.
That's what they thought, yes. That's what they thought. And so consequently --
You wouldn't have thought your school pals would have thought that though, would you?

The school kids? Oh, the school kids, they loved it, the kids. Because they all had a ball, you know, they went to clapping and that's the reaction that I think turned the teachers and the principal and everybody --
It was the teachers that didn't like it.

Yes. But the music teacher told me, he said, "Listen, I don't care what they say, listen. Don't pay that no mind." So I told him, I says, "Everybody in every class I go to, they got me sitting up there feeling bad and like I've done something real bad or something, know what I mean?" And even one of my cousins come by our house one night. He said, "Well, I heard J.C. got up there in school and played the lowdown dirty blues."
(Laughter.)

Told my folks. And you know, my folks don't want me playing it no way. So I just didn't do any playing to speak of with the exception of every once in a while, well, I would play in the church, you know, play church music, but I wasn't reading any music, but, you know, you go to church and you hear these songs and they're in your ear and that's the way I learned to play them, you know. And since there was no one there to play for Sunday school, if it'd be up to you, why, I'd go in there and play for them, you know? But nothing but church songs.
(Inaudible).

Oh, they was happy about that. So then I got to thinking, I says, why, every once in a while, I just want to get off to myself and play. So when Sunday come around, I'd get sick. I'd tell my folks, "Oh, I'm just so sick, I can't go to Sunday school." They say, "What's the matter?" I'd say, "I don't know. I ate something. My stomach is just hurting." And I'd fall on the floor, you know, and do my act, you know. So they say, "Put that boy to bed. Put him to bed." They'd give me something, you know. "You take this and take that. We all going to church now. We'll be back now." "All right." You know, as soon as I see them turn the corner, I'd go in there and sit down and play the piano.
(Laughter.)
And I'd just play, enjoy myself, you know? And I'd sit there and enjoy myself.
They spent a lot of hours in church, did they?

Well, you know, they go to Sunday school about 9:30 and then church at 11 and they'd get home at about 12:30 or 1:00. So finally, one old sister come by the house. She says, "Sister Mac, did you all go to church today?" She says, "Yeah, we all went to church. Everybody except the boy. The boy was sick, you know. He was feeling bad. He ate something, so he stayed here." "What was that I heard at your house?" She says, "I don't know, what?" She said, "Well, he might have been sick, but somebody was sure playing them wheels." Reels (?)
(Laughter.)

I knew I was in for trouble then. I was in for it. Because they'd realize right away I played sick to stay home and was playing the piano. "If he was playing that piano, he wasn't sick." So it was -- my grandmother, she could come over -- the only way I could get by with it was when my grandmother came by and my mother's mother. So she'd come by and say, "Son, play me some church songs." I'd play Dwelling in Beulah Land, you know, and those songs, you know, Nearer, My God, To Thee, and all that stuff. She'd sit up and pat her foot. So after a while, she'd turn around and say, "Now, look
here, play me some of that other music."
(Laughter.)

And I'd be so happy she said that, you know, and the folks, my old man, would be sitting, reading the paper, and I'd start that other stuff. He'd pull the paper back, but he wouldn't say nothing. My mother would come in there and look out at me. They wouldn't say nothing because I could hide behind grandma, you know.
(Inaudible).
And so that's the way I'd get a chance to do these other things, you know?
Jay, you know when you said your sister said he'd be playing those wheels. Is that what they called it? reels(?)
They called them reels in those days. Reels, which means bad music. Like blues, like, you know, see, they -- you know what I mean. Blues or --
Ragtime.
Yeah, ragtime, all that stuff. All of that was considered reels, you know.
Where in the world did they get that from?
I never did -- I never could understand (inaudible).
Because that was music that they
could dance to, like a reel.
Unless -- I don't know. I know they used to do some kind of dancing, they used to call the Virginia Reel, you know.
Yeah, that's --
That's the only thing about it. I imagine they figured as long as it's danceable, that was a reel, you know.
(Inaudible).
But it was funny.
(Laughter.)
So when did you first really be able to play some with all that opposition?
I'll tell you what happened. The --
Which school was this where you --
This was at Manual Training High School in Muskogee. So I'm getting around my senior year. I finished high school pretty young. I finished it at 16, and--
You were a good student.

Well, they thought I was. But the only thing that really helped me -- they thought I was a good student because during that time I would read and I never did do any studying. I did very little studying, but I did a lot of reading and I was lucky, whatever I was reading about, went along with classes and whatever they came up with, I was up on it, and that's how I -- you know what I mean. They thought
I was smart, but I wasn't.
You were smart to read.

It's lucky I was reading the right things, you know, and so anyway, that was getting around my, you know, senior year, and so this fellow Mr. Collins -- you know, the one that had practically forced me to play there in school, he told me he was going to get a little group together and he says, "I want you to play the piano." And he got saxaphone, I think he had two trumpets and a couple of saxophones and a bass and a drum, you know, and he put me on the piano, you know, so I told him, I said, "I don't know nothing about this stuff." He says, "That's all right. Just come on."

So then he says, "The first thing I'm going to do, I'm going to have rehearsals out to your house." He knew who my people were, you know. So he had the rehearsal out to my house and so they thought, "Well, you know, maybe this ain't too bad. You know, Mr. Collins, he's teaching there and he teaches music." He brought these guys out here and he had a drummer, you know, but my folks enjoyed watching him drum and he'd be doing all this stuff and you know how --
Everybody liked drums.
Yes, they enjoyed the drummer, you know. So they enjoyed the drummer and they would just sit and so they figured, "Well, maybe it wasn't too bad," you know,

so he told them, he says, "Now, we're probably going to play some Christmas jobs and you know," so I told him he'd better talk to them because I knew they wouldn't let me do it. So they said, "Well, if it's with you, it's all right. But if it was anybody else, we wouldn't let him play."
(Laughter.)
So we did. We did, I think, about three or four Christmas dates, you know, and --
You could bring a little money --

Made a little change. I don't know what we made. We made about 80 cents each day, I think, 80 or 90 cents. But the funniest thing about it, he would tell me, they'd start playing and I would be sort of listening, some tune that I didn't know. So he'd turn around and say, "Compliment the blues!" I didn't know what he was talking about. "Compliment the blues!" "Compliment the blues?" I said, I didn't know what that was, so I'd just start hitting notes that I thought would sound all right with them. He said, "That's what I'm talking about."
(Laughter.)

And I -- you know how you can be so dumbfounded and then you're founded, you know. So I said -- that was it. I says, "He sure had a funny way of telling me what to do." I said, "I didn't realize it was that easy," you know? So I finished high school and after finishing high school, I decided
I wanted to go to college. Well, I had a chance to go to Knoxville College, which is in Tennessee, and so there was another fellow there --
When you say you had the chance to go there, how was that?
Well, that came about -- they -- what do you call these little -- they call them grants now.
Scholarships?

Scholarships. So I wrote and told them I wanted to go to that college. So they said, 'If you want to go, we'll give you a scholarship that will take care of so much of your expense. But you'll have to come up with so much,' you know? So this fella named Jesse Culbertson and myself, we had both written there. So he had a scholarship and I had a scholarship.
What was the other guy's name?
Jesse Culbertson.
CULbertson?
Uh-huh. So he and I got a ride from Muskogee to Nashville, Tennessee with his uncle.
Was that Fisk?
Fisk was in Nashville.
Yeah, that wasn't where you were going.
No, we were going to Knoxville College.
Oh yeah.

But what we did though, I knew the lady used to teach me in the third grade, she was working at Fisk University. So I stopped by and hollered at her while we were in Nashville. So she told us, she said, 'Listen, fellas, this is where you want to go. You want to go to school here.' She says, 'This will be your best bet.'
Was Knoxville a white college?
It was a church college. I think everybody --
Oh, so (inaudible).
Yeah.
I see, right.

And so she was telling us -- she said, 'I'll tell you what I'll try to do.' She say, 'I can't get you no scholarship, but I'll get you guys a job, because a lot of the jobs comes through the office and if I can get you a job, then you can just make it, you know, scuffle and make it.'

So okay, we stayed around there, you know, and no jobs was coming through, no jobs, no jobs. I even went out for football. I says, 'Well, I got to do something, because they going to kick us out, you know.' No money come in. So we were lucky, we were staying with an old lady. We weren't staying on campus. We were staying with an old lady there that

gave us a room, you know, and I don't know what she was charging but it wasn't much. And so we was kind of having it a little rough, you know. So I went out, I said, "Well, I'll play some football." I went out, tried to make the team. I didn't realize there was so many other big guys out there, see, and I was only weighing about 140 pounds.
(Laughter.)

Those guys got through with me that afternoon. They hung me. So I even hurt my hand, you know, while I was out there. So in the meantime, next day, some fellows were trying to find somebody to play for a school party. Couldn't find nobody around there nowhere. So this Culbertson guy was with me, he told them, he said, "Well, I know a guy -- I don't know how many songs he knows, but I know he knows a couple of songs." They said, "Man, we want anybody. We don't care who it is. Just get anybody. If they don't know but one song or half a song, somebody. We got to have some music."

So he sent them up there to me, you know. So I said, "No, fellas, I couldn't play that." They said, "Do you know any songs at all?" I said, "I know about one or two songs." They said, "Well, you come on and you play them one or two songs all night, long as the party lasts, and we'll pay you." I said, "What?" They said, "We'll pay you." I said, "Okay."
(Laughter.)
You played the same song --

I played the same two and three songs over all night, you know. I did know more than those two or three, you know, to myself, feel that I could do just but two or three songs, but I played, you know, I played that night and I think they gave me 80 cents and they gave me 80 cents. Well, I hadn't had no money in my pocket for so long, you know, it was just, oh, boy.

So anyway, they called us up to the board. This fella says, "Well, now, there's nothing we can do for you." He says, "There's no jobs coming through and everything's bad." He says, "You're going to have to write your folks for some money." Well, I knew there was no money at home, you know, and his folks didn't have no money. So he and I decided, I says, "Well, look, we got to leave here." And we felt so bad about it, we didn't go back to see the lady, Mrs. Grimes, you know, the one who taught me in the third grade, we felt so bad about it, you know, because the officials had told us we got to go, you know.
So we caught a freight train and went to Knoxville.
(Laughter.)
So the guy told us, he says --
How far is that?
Knoxville is, oh, I'd say about 300 miles from there.
Had you ever caught a freight train before?
Had never caught one before. But we caught the freight and went to Knoxville.
Where did you ride on the thing? In a car or --

Well, sometimes -- you know those oil cars, you know, got the ring around them, you know? We'd stand up and ride those. Sometimes there was an open boxcar and we'd get in the boxcar if they wasn't traveling too fast. And sometimes when the special agents were bad on those trains, sometimes they'd shoot at you, you know.
Oh, they would shoot at you?

Oh, yes. So we'd get in those refrigerator cars, but we'd pull the inside lock inside and then pull the door down, so they couldn't lock us in. So we learned a lot of stuff in a hurry. We learned it fast.
(Laughter.)
Would they just shoot at you for being there?

Oh, yes. Oh, yes. Well, I'll tell you what happened. We had this to happen to us. See, after we got to Knoxville, things got tough again, so we decided there ain't nothing for us to do but go back home. So we left Knoxville, going back home, and we went into Chattanooga and

leaving Chattanooga, going through Nashville, you go through those Lookout Mountains, you know. Some people call them the Blue Mountains. And we were on this freight and the old guy put us off. Okay, put us off, so the next time we caught a car with a lot of junk in it, a lot of iron and stuff, iron ore and stuff. So we figured we'd hide down between there where they couldn't see us. So open the boxcar, you know, and that guy come through there and found us again --
The same guy?

Same guy. See, what we did, we let part of the train go by and then caught it again. So he told us, "I told you. Now next time, I'm going to shoot you." But we was determined to make it, so we let about eight or ten, 15 cars go by, and we got on it again.
(Laughter.)

We got on it again. We got in this refrigerator car, had no idea -- we knew we had it beat, you know, because when he came along that refrigerator car, he pulled the door open, he pulled it open. He says, "Here you are again." And he shot, you know. I imagine he probably shot in the air. I don't know what he shot, because he didn't hit us. But we jumped up out of there and we jumped -- we got out. So by that time, the end of the freight is gone. So we said, "Here we are." We walked about a mile. So we finally said, "There's no need to walk. We might as well just stop here

and maybe take us a nap and wait for the next freight to come by." So that's what we did. We waited until the next freight came by. So the next freight came by. Sometimes, you know, my buddy used to be a little bit slow about catching those freights, but I told him, I said, "Now look, this time don't be slow, because I don't want to have to leave you out here in these mountains. We both got to get it. You get it and I'm going to get it."
So we got it.
Did he get it ahead of you or something or did you each pick a car?

We'd each pick one, you know. There's a certain way that you catch that freight because you don't want to catch it on the -- you catch it on the front end that's coming to you on the -- I believe it's the right side, front end, not the lower end, because that will whip you all around, you know what I mean. You catch that front end, you can brace yourself.

So that's what we did. So we came on into Nashville. So we was ashamed to go out there to see Mrs. Grimes. But we went by the old lady's where we had stayed, because she told us -- she said, "The only thing I can do for you, fellas, I can fix you some bacon and eggs and send you on your way." So she did. She fixed bacon and eggs and we went on and rode all the way back to Oklahoma on the freight. And so quite
naturally, when you get back home and we just felt bad, you know, it was a bad feeling.
Yeah, you failed.

Failure, you know. So finally, we did get a letter from Mrs. Grimes later on. She says, 'Fellas, I know you was having a hard time and I know what you was going through.' She says, 'But if you had just held out two more weeks, because some jobs did come in, I was going to hold these jobs definitely for you all.' But anyway, that was over with. That episode was through. So I came in home that night, you know how you do, all soot -- soot was all over me from the train, hitting you and that smoke, you know, and the coal dust.
Soot.

Yeah. So I didn't know how to go in the house, you know. The old dog was just barking. He just kept barking. So they come back out and somebody come out there and turned the back light on, look around, and I was hiding behind the side of the house and I'd come back out and the old dog went to barking again. So I figured, I said, 'I might as well go on in.' So my sisters, they had a few friends over to the house, you know, and I walked in and the first thing they did, 'Well, look here. Look at him. Look at him, he looks like a tramp. Look at the tramp that's shown up.' You know what I mean? Oh, man. You know, and their
friends came around and was looking me over, you know.
(Laughter.)

My mother said, "Oh, what happened to you?" I said, "Well, we couldn't make it, so we had to take a freight home." She said, "Well, get in there and get in that tub." That was the first thing she -- you know what I mean? So I cleaned up. But after I was home two days or three days, you know, see, I had got the fever, see, and I didn't want to stay home. So I told my dad, I said, "Well, I'll tell you what. I just got to get out of here. I got to go somewhere and do something."
(Inaudible)?

Well, I'm still 16. He said, "Well, where are you going to go?" I said, "Well, my uncle in Tulsa. I'll go over there and see if I can get a job over there." He said, "Well, okay. If you can't make it, drop me a line. I'll get you back home." You know. He says, "I hate to see you come back on the freight like you did. If it gets bad --" you know. So I went on over to Tulsa and I walked streets about two weeks and wasn't a job doing nothing. You couldn't get a job doing anything. So finally --
Was this Depression time?

Yes, this was during the Depression. And so one day, I heard a band playing and heard the music. So I followed the music, you know, kept following the sound. Kept following it until I came to a place and I could tell the band

was upstairs playing. It was Al Denny. His band was rehearsing. He had about a 12-piece band. So I went upstairs, just walked on in, went upstairs and sat down and listened to him. They didn't have a piano player. So I heard the musicians talking, "We don't know what we're going to do for a piano player." Said, "We got to do something. We got to get one from somewhere." So finally, I walked up to the guy after I heard him play these songs. I said, "Man, I think I can make it." He said, "You can make it? You a piano player?" I says, "Yeah, I think I can make it." He said, "Well, come on, get on up." So I got on up. I sat down. They put all this orchestration in front of me, you know. I just went along with the band, you know, playing. He said, "Oh, man, we got a cat can read and fake." They thought I was reading.
(Laughter.)

They told me to take a solo and I just went on and so they said, "Oh, man, he can read and fake. Man, we got -- man, why didn't you say something. Why were you sitting down there for?" You know. So that -- I started working with Al Denny's band and then I worked with Al Denny up until a fellow came to town named Lee Dare (PHONETIC). He was looking for some musicians. Used to be some brothers called the Gray Brothers -- they had a band.
What was his name, Jay?
Lee Dare.
: JAY, just before you get that far, now seriously, I mean, you weren't playing piano everyday at home or anywhere.
No.
: Well, I mean, exactly what kind of a repertoire did you have when you sat down with Al Denny's band? What were they playing? Stock arrangements?
They were playing stocks.
: On regular tunes?
On tunes.
: 'Honeysuckle Rose,' stuff like that?
Uh-huh, whatever, you know, 'Kansas City Kitty.' Let me see, what were some of these other tunes? Tunes like 'Judy,' you know --
(Inaudible).
Yeah, like that.
: And in every case, you just played the chords.
Just went right along with them, whichever way they went, you know?
: And the tunes, you could retain them.
I could retain them. Well, you know, you happen to hear something new to retain.
: Yeah.
So it's no trouble. You set it in
there one time and it's there, you know?
(Laughter.)
Well, listen, so you'd get a chance to go for yourself, what would you do? Just sort of play that melody?
Oh, you mean when they'd tell me to play the solo?
Yes.

Oh, yes. I played the melody like I wanted to play it. I just played the way that I wanted to play it and then when the band came back in and I could go on back with the "boom-chink, boom-chink, boom-chink," which was the beginning of the "complimenting the blues."
(Laughter.)
But it says here, Jay, that you were with that band for four months. Is that right? With Al Denny?
How's that?
You were with Al Denny -- was it Dennis or Denny?
D-e-n-n-i-e, Dennie.
D-e-n-n- --
i-e.
i-e.
Uh-huh.
They've got Dennis here.
Yeah, it was Dennie. Yeah, he was -- a lot of times, they make mistake on the --
Yeah. But when you (unintelligible) spent two months as Fisk. Had you been at Fisk?
We didn't spent two months, we spent about a month there, about a month.
Yeah.
Yeah, it was about a month there, see, because we didn't have -- we just didn't have enough money to carry us.
Who was it though you told me you used to raid the landlady's refrigerator?
Oh, that was later on when I was in junior college, when I used to raid the landlady's frigidaire.
(Laughter.)
So after Al Dennie, this man -- what was his name again?
Lee Deere.
Lee Deere. How is Deere spelled?
D-e-e-r-e.
D-e-a-r-e.
D-e-e-r-e.
He comes to Tulsa?
Yes, he came there looking for some

musicians. Now, Lee Deere, he was a fella that always wanted to be in the nightclub business, he and his brother, and also he had some friends named Babe and Clyde Burton. They -- well, you know how it was in the days when it was dry in Kansas. So they was the two guys that --
(End of Tape One, Side One.)
All right. Lee Deere.

Yes, Lee Deere was a -- quite a nightclub operator, he and his brother, Walt Deere, and they was known throughout Kansas, Wichita and little towns where they would have nightclubs and whatnot. They were very good friends of Clyde and Babe Burton. So Lee Deere came to town to pick up the Gray Brothers, which they were all working in a group. Gene Calloway was with that group, Oscar Williams on drums. One Gray brother, Hunter Gray, played alto, Henry playing the trumpet. And he also had Art Bronson, you know, a piano player, Art Bronson, working at this club for him.
Bronson? How do you spell that?
B-r-o-n-s-o-n.
Yeah, I've heard of him.
Art Bronson used to have a big band in Denver. He had a good guys like Lester Young and all those type of guys. In fact, this is -- you know, I'm first to kind of getting around some guys, you know?
Yeah.

And so Lee Deere told me, he says, 'Look, I can take you up to play piano for some friends of mine, but Art Bronson is playing at my club, but see, I'd like to have you with these guys here. But Art's playing at my club. But if you go,' he says, 'I'll guarantee you $14 a week and you'll make good tips.' I said, 'Oh,' I didn't believe it, you know. He says, 'Yes, I'll guarantee it, yes.' So then I got to thinking. I said, Well, I think I'll take this,' you know?
Well, listen, Jay, I'm a little muddled. Art Bronson was playing with the group he came to take?

Well, Art had maybe three or four guys up there he had been using. But, see, they wanted this band those musicians, like the saxophone player, the trumpet player, the drummer, and the girl that -- well, they didn't want the girl that played piano, but all the rest of the band and the other -- you know, like you come into a club and take a whole band out of what you want?
Yeah.
So that's what they were really doing, you know?
And so they were asking you to come on piano?
No, the boys knew me. Hunter Gray,

the Gray brothers, and they knew that he was also looking for a piano player for his friends. So they called me and says, "How about making this? We going," which was in Arkansas City, Kansas. So I was staying with my uncle and aunt in Tulsa, and she was just as strict as my parents, more strict, you know.
Was this uncle your mother's brother or your father's brother?

My father's brother. And so she came up, she says, "Who are those people?" I says, "They are from up in Kansas." She says, "What did they want?" I says, "They offered me a job." She says, "Well, what did you tell them?" I said, "I told them I'd leave with them." She said, "You're not leaving." I said, "Oh, yeah. I'm leaving."
(Laughter.)

She says, "No, you're not. I'm going to call your dad and mother right now." She got on the phone and while she was on the phone, I had my clothes and they drove up and I just left with them, before she ever got them on the phone. So I left and went to Arkansas City and I worked with a guy up there called S. C. Henderson. Now he was an old-timer. See, and I'm just sort of getting, you know what I mean, and I learned a lot of tunes that -- he knew tunes that I didn't know, like we would get requests, but I would learn them because I would tell him to go ahead and do them on his guitar and I'd play along with him. That's the way I learned these

tunes that I didn't know, tunes like, 'This town is full of guys who think they mighty wise,' 'Ace in the Hole,' those kinds of tunes. So those were considered money tunes, you know? You know, certain tunes that these guys -- the gamblers would come in to hear, you know, and the other guys would come in to hear certain tunes. Well, we called them, they called them money tunes.
Because they tip.
Because they'd tip for those tunes.
And so --
What was this guitar player's name again?
Essie Henderson.
How do you spell the Essie?
E-s-s-e. And he was an old-timer.

Now, he'd been around with guys, you know, when I heard him talk about so many older musicians I'd heard talk about, but I'd never met him, you know. But anyway, Lee Deere took his group up there and I went to work over here with Essie at this other club, see? And that was -- I really got a lot of experience right there, you know, and part of the experience that, you know, I got from just sitting there with Essie and then I'd go out and these guys, they would also get music, you know, because Lee Deere, he believed in keeping everything right up to date. If you remember Lee Deere, he was the guy
that not too long ago, he owned the Thunderbird in Vegas.
Oh, yes, you told me that.
That was Lee Deere. And he --
So he really stayed in the business.
Yes, he really stayed in the business, yes, he did.
Well, Jay, if you had to fill in with the guitar, you had to do a lot more filling in that you would have to do with a band.
That's right, I did.
(Inaudible).
Uh-huh. Well, that's really what happened. It helped me a lot because with just the two of us there, we had, you know, we had --
I mean, you don't get much melody off the guitar.
That's right. And so I -- that's when after they closed the club there in that particular town --
What was the name of that club?
What would they call it? That was -- let me see, that was the Cedars Club that Lee Deere had. And they just called it the Burton Brothers Club when I was there, you know, Burton Brothers Club.
When you mentioned Clyde Burton, who was he?
Clyde Burton?
Didn't you say -- who did you say --
Clyde Burton and Babe Burton. Those were the two fellas I worked for, the two brothers.
Oh, I see. Were they well known for anything besides running this place?
Well, I imagine they run a lot of booze in their days and things like that.
Well, you spoke of them as though they were kind of important.
Well, to the going people, people that go to clubs and things like that, they were well known. They were, you know, like club people, they says, "Well, I'm going out to Babe's," you know.
Yeah.

And then you really get a chance to see how well known they were, you know, as well as Lee Deere being so well known. So they had consequently, they had the town wrapped up and there never were anybody else come in there and making the competition.
(Laughter.)
What town was it?
That was Arkansas City, Kansas. That's not too far from the line of Oklahoma. And it's about 60 miles south of Wichita.
: Well, (inaudible)?
Arkansas City must have been about 15 or 16,000.
15 to 16,000, population.
: Not very big.
It might have been a little bit bigger, but not much.
: What made that a sort of lively place?

Well, what made that lively -- you see, there was a lot of people that used to come down there from Winfield, Kansas. Winfield is about 18 or 20 miles north of there and there was a lot of people that come up from Oklahoma and there was Newkirk, Oklahoma, Ponca City, Oklahoma. These little towns. So consequently they had a lot of drawing power, see, because they could get by running these places -- all of this was dry states.
: All dry, was it?
All dry, Oklahoma and Kansas.
: (Inaudible)?
Yes. So people that was wanting someplace to go, they wanted somewhere that they could go to

drink and they wanted somewhere, you know, to meet -- and we just, you know what I mean, and so they just wanted somewhere to go to spend money and these guys were lucky enough, they was able to get off with it. I guess they were probably paying off, I don't know, evidently. Had to be.
Why -- didn't federal people raid them?
Oh, yes, they got raided. But I think it was a nice thing they had going. You know, if --
They had (inaudible).

Yes. If they were going to get raided, they'd call them and tell them ahead of time. So consequently, they'd always let them find a little something. Leave a little something out for them to find and take down for evidence, but not that much, you know, because they was already waiting for these guys, you know, when they come there. "Okay, come on in. Check it over." And check it over and the guys get on back out. They'd open up the next day. Well, they'd take so and so down and take him down for a little while, stay overnight, be right back in business the next day.
(Laughter.)
So that's the way that went on. So I decided I wanted to go back to school, you know, after the club closed.
Well, had you saved up some money now?
I'd saved up some money then.
Well, I'd like to know how your thinking was then. So by then, you'd been playing music for about a year, I guess, had you or more?
Right.
And you just -- you loved the life, I guess.

Well, I'll tell you the truth, I didn't drink a thing. People couldn't understand. They said, "I've never seen a musician that didn't drink." People would come in the clubs and would want to buy me a drink, you know, I just didn't drink and people didn't -- you know, they just couldn't understand it. So finally, I met some girl, you know, there in Arkansas City, and so-she told me, "I want to invite you to a party." She says, "But now, when you come to the party, the party will start about the time after you all get off from work. But when you come to the party, I want you to bring some whisky." Well, I don't know nothing about no whiskey, you know?

So I told the guy that night that I'm working for, Babe Burton, I says, "Look, I'm supposed to go to a party. They want me to bring some whiskey. What would you suggest?" He said, "Well, I got some Four Roses here." And that sounded good to me, Four Roses. Oh, I said, "Four Roses?"
Always sounds good.
(Laughter.)
I thought, "Well, that's what I want."

So he gave me, I guess it might have been a pint of Four Roses. So I'm a big man tonight, you know. Big man. They come by and pick me up and, "Girls, we've got Four Roses tonight. This is Four Roses. Don't forget. This is Four Roses." Oh, boy. Everybody else was older than I was. They were more experienced, you know, and I guess they could tell. They said, "Well, we got a jay hawk here, you know what I mean."
But anyway, everybody -- nobody got high but me.
(Laughter.)

Sick, you know. So that was sort of my first to getting exposed to the booze, you know, and of course, I had gotten exposed earlier in my high school year at one time, because I played for a party for some lawyer and I even rode my bicycle to the gig and after the gig, came home.
(Laughter.)
I couldn't even put the bicycle on the porch, I was so, you know. But when I came in the house, I came in and I just got deathly sick and laid across the bed and everything came up, you know.
What had you been drinking then?

I think they gave me a little booze that night. It didn't have to be much because, you know, I didn't know anything about it. And so I heard my mother tell my dad, she says, "You know, I smell whiskey." He said, "Oh,
it's somebody in the neighborhood making it." She said, "No, this smells like it's coming from that boy's room."
(Laughter.)
He says, "Oh, go on back to sleep now. That's some of the bootleggers in the neighborhood." She says, "Well, I'm going to get up and look."
(Laughter.)
She got up and turned the light on. She said, "Oh, my goodness. Look what this devil has done."
(Laughter.)

She says, "Oh, get up right now. Get up, get out of this bed and clean this up." Oh, I was so sick. She made me get up and clean it up. So I figured, I said, "Well, I know it's going to be something else tomorrow." "I'm going to have your daddy to get on you. I'm going to have him to skin you alive."

So the next day, the old man told me, "Come here, boy. Listen, now, you go to these places here. You tell them to give you something like punch. Don't give you none of that other stuff." I said, "Okay, that's what I'll do." So that was the end of that. That's all he ever said to me, you know?
: Were you drinking it straight or what were you doing?
Well, they had it mixed, but you know, when you have never had that stuff, it hits your stomach and

it's just boom, you know? Yeah. I can remember the very first time I smoked cigarettes. I went home and I went in the back door, felt terrible, but didn't know what was bothering me. Threw up on the kitchen floor and my mother came in, and she could smell it. I don't know what -- what was it in those days you used to get your fingers stained with?
Oh, that was tobacco.
Yeah, I know, but --
Nicotine.
Nicotine.
I know it was the nicotine, but certainly people used to get stains on their fingers much more. But now, they --
Yes, you don't get stains like you did then. And then they used to chew tobacco, you know?
Yes.
They'd chew tobacco, you know, and --
Did you ever try that?

I tried that. See, I used to work at a little old grocery store and every Saturday night, you know, that's my night to have myself a party, you know. I'd work at this grocery store and so Saturday night, I'd goto town. I'd walk to town. But before I'd leave the grocery store, I'd go by and check, 'Let me see. I'll get a little piece of this
tobacco, cut that off, put it in my pocket. Get some candy over here. Look over there and get me a couple of cigars," you know, loading up.
(Laughter.)
I'd go to town, walk all the way to town, a mile and a half, thought nothing of it, walked a mile and a half --
This was at home?
In Muskogee. Smoke my cigar and on the way back from town, chew on tobacco. I'd come in so sick and drunk, I wouldn't know what to do. But I'd come in and go straight to bed.
That chewing tobacco, I mean, that will make you throw up.
Oh, it will kill you. It will. That was the worst I ever had. I left the cigars alone then and I left tobacco alone. That was it. And I let them go.
That chewing tobacco, I mean, once that gets down your throat. I don't know how people manage it.

I never could understand it, because there was a lot of people I used to see and people would come in that store there and after my episode, I couldn't understand how they could handle it. They'd say, "Give me some store tobacco. Give me Brown's Mule." "Give me so on and so on." I'd look at them -- but I don't know, people, I guess their con-
stitution was a lot different.
No, I think there must be some sort of technique to that, chewing tobacco, because you know, probably they don't let it get down their throat.
Well, that could be the thing, because they put it over here or down here or --
They spit when they --
Yeah, everytime you'd look around, that's what they would be doing, you know?
But I could never understand the way they dip snuff, either.
Well, you know --
Did you do that?
I never did try that, because, first of all, I hate to see my grandmother dip snuff. I hated to see her dip snuff and so I hated to see her dip snuff, I just never had the nerve to try it.
Why did you hate to see her? Did it look bad or --

Yes. You know, and sometime I'd say, well, you know, you have to be careful how you talk to the old folks sometime. I said -- I used to call her -- she's my grandmother, but I always called her Mammy, you know, I called her Mammy, because I could get more out of her by calling her Mammy, you know. If I called her Grandmother,
that's all right for the girls to call her Grandmother, but she didn't want me to call her Grandmother, you know, and you know what I mean.
Yeah.

But I'd call her Mammy and I'd say it real forceful like, and she liked that, you know, and I used to -- that's when I found out, when I found out what she liked, well, then, that's when I used to have her cook me different kinds of cakes and things, you know, and then she -- it had just got to be a ritual with her. Every birthday, I had to have that cake, see, because I'd make over it so.
(Laughter.)
So --
(Inaudible).
You started to say though, --
Yeah, see, (unintelligible), tell her, I says, "Look," I said --
It's like people who have a beard or a mustache, you know, people who sniff snuff get yellow marks on their mustahces.
That's true.
It looks horrible.
It does.
But what did you say to her?
I'd tell her, I'd say, "Grandma,

there's something running down there near your mouth." "What?" "There's something running down there near your mouth. I don't know what it is. So maybe you better wipe it off." "Oh, it ain't nothing but snuff." "Oh, well, I didn't know. I didn't think you'd want to --" give a little shrug, you know. "Okay." You know, long as I did it that way, you know.
(Laughter.)
And I had to be very careful how I said it, you know.
So after you had your job, you'd already been indoctrinated into this on the whiskey and the tobacco. You turned off for a while.
Yes, that's true. And so then I decided. I said, "Well, I'm going to go to school." So I went to junior college.
But you thought (inaudible).
Well, I always had a -- wanted to go to school. I don't know why I had it, you know, but I did, and so I went to junior college.
Where was that?
This was still in the same town, Arkansas City.
How did you have the money?
He saved it.
Well, I had saved it, you see. I had worked, you know, and I had worked and I had saved my money and

so then I went on to junior college. But you see now, after you're in college about a year and a half, see, your money's running out, see? Because they close the town up and there was nowhere for me to play. Couldn't make no money nowhere, you know. And the only thing --
Well, by closed up, do you mean Prohibition had gotten the better of things? (Inaudible).
Yes, when they -- you know, they completely closed Babe Burton up and Lee Deere --
They'd gone on top of the booze.

Yeah, so that there was nobody operating and that's when I sometimes would go down to this town I was telling you about, Ponca City, and playing maybe one night a week or two nights for Alligator, you know.
How do you spell that, Ponca City?

P-o-n-c-a. Ponca City. And that's the reason, you know, I ran into that stuff down there. I'd go down and play maybe one or two nights for Alligator, but then I'd have to take the bus and go down and wait and catch another bus late in the morning and come back, you know?
What were you studying at this junior college?
Oh, just studying, just regular course, just regular college course.
You weren't sort of specialized in

Didn't specialize in anything. And it was a drawback because I didn't have any -- for me, what I wanted was an instrument, but I didn't have no instrument, so that was a drawback to me. Otherwise, I could have gotten into school, just with a school band, you know, which I really wanted to do. But sometimes I would borrow a fella's, he had a clarinet and I used to borrow his clarinet. And went over there to the school band, you know, but that didn't last too long because his folks made him bring his clarinet in, you know what I mean?

So anyway, that's where I started raiding the people's ice box. Things got tough, you know, and I wasn't making any money. So I didn't have no money and so I'd go on down there and check the old girl's ice box to see what she had, you know.
(Laughter.)
After she'd gone to sleep.

Yeah. Wait until she'd grow to sleep. So then, she told me, she says, 'Look, I'll tell you what. Mack, now, you have been raiding this ice box for the last two weeks. Now,' she says -- her son was playing with Eddie Hill's band in Shawnee, Oklahoma. She says, 'Now, why don't you just forget about this school.' And so I told her, 'Well, I'd like to stay here and finish up my exam, which would have been about another month or another four or five weeks, and she says,

"Well, I'll tell you what. I was just down there and saw my son," which was playing with this band." She says, "And they need a piano player. Now you're not doing no good here." She says, "I just suggest that you go on down there and tell Eddie that I'm going down tomorrow, that you're ready to come." I said, "Well, okay, just send me a ticket and $3."
(Laughter.)
And $3, because I wanted to get something to eat.
Yeah.
He did, he sent me the ticket and $3 and I went to a chili joint and sit down and just took my time and had a feast on chili.
(Laughter.)
And I went down and then I joined this group down there.
Which group is this?
This was Eddie Hill.
Oh, yeah.
Eddie Hill and his Bostonians and there was nobody in there from Boston.
(Laughter.)
And what town was that?
That was Shawnee, Oklahoma. And we were playing there to an old ballroom that had been there for years. Benny Moten and all the guys used to play there, you

know? Bluebird Ballroom. And so we played there, I think it was either three or four nights a week and then sometimes we'd play a dance for one of those small towns or something like that and that went along up until some fellow came from Albuquerque, New Mexico, looking for a band, you know. Of course, --
How many pieces was this band?
Huh?
How many pieces --
had about eight or nine-piece band.
And you said some different guys were playing in that band, the one that you said Lester and --
Other band.
Well, no, this wasn't the band that Lester played. That was Art Bronson's band that Lester --
Oh, I see.
-- and a lot of -- he had a lot of good musicians.
Anybody we'd know in Eddie Hill's band?
Well, yes, the Gray Brothers that had worked for Lee Deere, they was in Eddie's band. And let me see now, who else was in that band? And Lester Taylor, he was in that band.
What did he play?
He played saxophone. That was his mother's house I was staying at, raiding the ice box.
(Laughter.)
Oh, he had about eight-piece band and so we got this chance to go to Albuquerque, New Mexico.
What would this band have been playing mostly? Stocks or --
Well, they were playing stocks, but then Eddie could arrange.
Oh.
He could arrange. He could write and arrange.
What was his instrument, Eddie Hill's?
Trumpet.
Oh.

And he was the guy that had been on the shows, you know, old show musicians and run a lot of good show musicians. He had been with So then he could write and then this Lester Taylor was doing some writing, you know.
Well, could most of the guys in this band read all right?
Well, they could spell fairly good, the spelling, you know, because between Lester and Eddie, they could get them through it and once they got them through it,
they had it, you know, and that's how the band moved along, you know, and so we all loaded up and went out to Albuquerque.
How far -- oh, I know how far that was.
That was a pretty good little town.
Yeah.
And so we worked there in Albuquerque there at a place called Silvas Resort.
Silvas?
Uh-huh.
Spell that.
S-i-l-v-a-s.
Silvas.
Yes.
Silvas what? What was that?
Resort.
Oh, resort.

This was right in the mountains and we were east of Albuquerque. You know -- you've been in Albuquerque, those mountains that you see due east of Albuquerque, that's where this resort was. Of course, now, back then, that was a long ways.
That's a bit breath-taking up in those mountains, isn't it?
Oh, yes, yes.
Was it like up in those mountains?
Well, we were right in the mountains.
Oh, you were?

Yes, right in the mountains, and because, as you leave from where we were, you go downhill all the way into town, all the way into Albuquerque and we -- they was getting the band together pretty nice. So this was giving me a little -- you know, was giving a chance to have a little experience, you know. I was getting --
You were learning to do reading, weren't you?
No, I --
You hadn't got to that?

No, I hadn't. In fact, I just -- you know, didn't take time. I would have learned to have read in a minute if I had a horn. But I just wouldn't take time -- well, you see, on the piano, you got a bass clef, you got a treble clef. You got two different clefs. And I didn't want to take the time to figure out this bass clef and to figure out this other clef. I figured if I had a horn, I'd read one line and I'm through, you know.
If you ever had played a horn, what horn would you fancy?

Well, I wanted a trumpet at first and after I couldn't get the trumpet, I told them I'd settle for a clarinet and then I told them I'd settle for alto or anything, but it was just -- they just never had the money

and while -- you see, the thing about it, I could do on practically any instrument as good as I could do on piano, like just starting out on piano, you know. I could pick up an instrument and just like -- pick up an instrument just like and start with a piano, you know, I guess I had a feeling for them, you know.
You could find the notes?

Yes. Could find them. And so, we worked out there in the mountains and I was -- I enjoyed working out in the mountains because I had always had asthma, you know, as a kid coming up, and I didn't realize it. While out in those mountains -- must have cured me, and I had no idea that was what was happening, but --
It was good air.
Good air. And out in those mountains and everything and so I really enjoyed it. But --
Did it cure the asthma though permanently or what?
Not permanently, because it's back now. Now I wheeze. I've been wheezing now for about the last year and a half.
What do you think has caused that to come back then?
Well, that -- well, my sinus. See, my sinus and then the sinus can hit you from so many directions
and the sinus hit me from so many different directions plus allergies, you know, and that's --
I mean, does smoking aggravate --
And that's bad.
That aggravates it.
That is bad. There's no question about it.
Also, I mean, playing in a smoky place.
That's true. And then when you stop and think about it, you've been playing a lot of years of your life in these places where there's smoke and you know what I mean?
Terrible.
It will take its toll.
Sure.

And I'm sure that's what brought it back, you know what I mean, which today, now I wheeze and then -- so I take these pills for congestion and so forth like that. Well, it's just a matter -- for that night, okay, maybe the next two nights, you might not, but the next thing you know, you're wheezing right back again, you know?
Yeah, that's too bad because, you know, that's a very bad thing that gets hold of you.
That's true. Yes, it is. So we stayed

out there in Albuquerque and it was going pretty nice with the exception, the fella that we was playing for, he and his wife, they -- she was really a young woman, she was a young woman and he was an older fella. And they used to kind of spat, you know, this white couple, you know, and they'd kind of have these spats and sometimes, I remember one time he got so mad at her, he started to cut her with a knife and we grabbed him, you know. "Oh, don't do that. Don't do that." You know. So then he used to talk to me a lot. He'd say, "I'll tell you what," he says, "Now, I know that I was acting up the other night. But don't pay that too much attention. I probably had a few hits there," he says, "you know, when I'm kind of acting up, I'm glad that you guys did talk to me." I said, "Well, we didn't want you to hurt her," you know, and so forth.

So then she got mad and put him out and he moved in town, Albuquerque. So he moved in town and so he -- when I'd go in town, sometime he'd call me up. He knew where I'd stop when I'd go in town. He'd call me up and say, "Look, how are things going out to the club?" I'd say, "Things are going pretty good." He'd say, "Well, I'll tell you what I want you guys to do. I want you guys -- I got a club I can put you all in in Phoenix. I want you all to leave that club. That place ain't no good out there. I want you to get away from there." I say, "Okay, well, listen, I'll tell Eddie to get in touch with you right away, because I'd like to go to Phoenix. I've never
been to Phoenix, you know." He said, "Well, you tell Eddie to get in touch with me." So, okay, I told Eddie. I think Eddie was kind of sweet on the girl, the old lady, see what I mean?
Yeah.

So Eddie ain't about to go nowhere. So the old man called me and said, "Did you tell Eddie?" I said, "Yeah, I told him." I says, "I tell you what. If Eddie don't want to go, you just -- you give the gig to me and I'll tell the rest of the guys. We'll make the gig."

So the old man says, "Well, if he don't call in pretty soon, I might just do that. I'll just give the gig to the rest of you guys and you all can go and make a date." So this friend of his, he said, had a club out there. Well, so, we had a big doings out there one night. Oh, the place was just loaded from front to back.
How big a place was it?
It was a big place.
I mean the resort.
The resort? Well, the resort, actually, the only thing that was happening at the resort, they had like adobe houses and where people could -- you know what I mean?
Were they up there riding houses and things?
No, they didn't have no horse riding.
Oh, it wasnt a dude ranch.
The only thing we had to offer was dancing, booze and the club.
Oh, I see. So it was like a sneak-away place.
Yeah.
I got you.
But it was a big place, you know, and the old man quite naturally, you know, he was crazy about this young woman and he had -- you know what I mean -- spent a lot of money on this place.
Yeah, yeah.

So we had this big doings there and oh, boy, just people from everywhere were there. So we got through playing that night and I decided to go in town, you know, and I went on in town. So the old man called me that next morning and he says, "Hey, how was things out at the club last night?" I says, "Oh, they was jumping. It was great." He says, "Well, now, listen, I'll tell you. You didn't have no trouble out there?" I says, "No, there wasn't no trouble." He says, "Well, I heard there had been some trouble out there." He says, "I figured I'd call you and check you out to see if there was." I said, "No, no, there wasn't no trouble." He says, "Okay," and he hung up. He went out on to the club.

But what happened, he went out to the club and he walked in, you know, in front of the club, went around to the side, you know, where they had sleeping quarters there, and they also had a house over there where they slept, he and the old lady, you know. So he walked in over here in the club. Well, Eddie Hill was in there with his old lady.
So, when she heard him walking through there, she pulled the thing over Eddie, pulled -- you know, and Jim walked in and looked --
Where were they?
In bed.
In bed.
Oh, in bed. I see, yeah.

Jim walked on back to the car, went and got his .45 and come on back in there and she went to running and says, 'Oh, Jim, Jim, Jim, don't kill him. Don't kill him.' Well, in the meantime, Eddie had some brand new shoes he'd bought. He picked them shoes and clothes up and ran. See, the mountain goes right up, you know, and run up that mountain and so the old man was looking for Eddie and he's running all around there trying to find Eddie. He shot her.
He did shoot her?
Uh-huh.
Did he do her in?
Huh?
Did he kill her?

Yes, see, she was out -- she come outside the club, see, and he shot her and he run around the club, looking for Eddie, and then he come back and shot her again. Then he pulled the pistol on himself. They couldn't find Eddie. Pulled the pistol on himself. About five minutes see, and I had already called out there, there was two or three guys that was cleaning up the place, and I called them and asked them, 'You all didn't have no trouble out there after I come in town?' They said no. About five minutes, they called me back and said, 'Man, yes, we did have some trouble, just now. Old man Jim come out and killed her and has killed himself and he's running up there trying to find Eddie.'

And then when he shot himself the second time, he fell right over her, you know. So consequently, the musicians inside, two of them cleaning up, all this commotion's going on, they was running over each other, running under the tables and everything else. So they called me and I said, 'Well, I'll be right back out.' So I come on back out. So by the time I got back out there, Eddie done come by the mountains and Eddie was crying, 'Oh,' and I looked at them shoes and they was wore out.
(Laughter.)
I said, 'Man, how did you wear out a pair of brand new shoes?'
(Laughter.)

But really, back to all seriousness. He came back, he says, 'Oh, man,' Eddie was crying and carrying on. I said, 'First thing you got to do is cut that out. Now we got to start thinking.' So the commissioner of the town, he had a night club. So in about a half an hour, he showed up out there. So he says, 'Man, this is awful. Do you know, you guys liable to have all kinds of trouble. Tell you what you all got to do, you all come on over and go to work for me and you all get Eddie Hill out of town,' you know.
The word was out, huh?

The word was out. So that night, we says, 'Okay -- ' Her mother was over to the other big house, you know. When her mother found out what happened, her mother cut her own throat. Now, this is all that's happening. Her mother cut her throat and her dad was just coming in from Denver and when he come in and seen everything that happened, first, he was questioning about the money. He says, 'Who got the money?' He thought it was some Mexican fella got the money. He didn't like this Mexican guy. I never will forget this guy's name, the guy's name was Nestor. You know, he did not like this Mexican bartender.
He told me, 'Jay, I know Nestor got that money.' I
Well, the money was gone, was it?

The money was gone, but the reason I knew Nestor didn't get it, Nestor never showed up out there after he left that night, see? Nestor never showed.
