But I did know this guitar player, he kept telling me, he says, "Mack, let's go." I said, "Go where?" "Let's go to Oklahoma City." I said, "Man, I ain't got but $30 in the bank and I ain't going to --" in the post office -- and I says, "--and I ain't going to take that out and pay my way to Oklahoma City when I got a job to do on here. He says, "You don't have to pay your way. I'll pay it." And he's going to pay a couple of other guys' way. Then I knew where the money was. You know.

So the old man, he come over and sit and talk, says, "Well, who do you think got the money?" Well, this guitar player and a couple of other guys, they went on back. We stayed, see? So I just told him, "No, Nestor didn't get it. I'll stand all day and tell you, all night, that Nestor did not get that money." I says, "Now, the other guys, they're gone. But I know Nestor didn't do it."

So anyway, the old man, he told me, "I'm hurt. I'm hurt. I've never felt like this in my life," and so on and so on and the old man went in the bathroom and blew his brains out. I said, "Well, I done seen everything now." One,
two, three, four.
The woman, her husband, hermother and then did he commit suicide, the father?
The father, that was the last one.
What did he do?
Huh?
Did he shoot himself?
He told me, he said, 'I've never felt like this. I don't know what to do.' And so then we went on, started playing for this commissioner of Albuquerque --
Well, who 'we?'
It was Hunter Gray left, Henry Gray, Oscar Williams on drums. We had a great big guy named Homer Woods played the bass horn. He was an old-timer.
Well, what did Eddie Hill do?
Huh?
What did Eddie Hill do?
Well, we got the money from the commissioner and put him on the bus that first night and sent him on to Los Angeles, either Los Angeles -- somewhere in California, you know.
Is he still around?
I never did find out what ever happened to Eddie. He wrote one letter back there to us, said he got there okay, and I never heard anymore from Eddie since.
And the guitar player and a couple more, they went to Oklahoma City?
They went on back to Oklahoma City and I know that he's the one that got the money, the guitar player.
(Laughter.)

Oh, boy, you know what I mean. Because after I put it all together, you know, and because he wanted to pay my way, you know. He said, 'Oh, I'll pay your way. You don't have to touch your money.' I said, 'Well, man, we got a job here to go on. You going to stand on the job?' 'No, no.' But we went to work for the county commissioner. He had a club down there and also Howard McGee was there.
In whose band?
Came in right after that.
Oh, in Eddie Hill's place?
No, he didn't come in Eddie's place, but he came in town -- oh, not long, right after this episode that happened.
And where did he go to work?
He went to work with us.
Oh, he did?
Uh-huh. Howard came in and went to work with us and --
Where did Howard come from?
Oklahoma. Yes, he's from -- I don't know what town, but he's from Oklahoma. But I think he gives Muskogee, doesn't he?
I think so. I don't know whether he's old enough.
In fact, I saw Howard, you know, in the Berlin Festival, oh, just -- what was that? A couple of months ago, right?
Born in Tulsa.
Huh?
He was born in Tulsa.
Tulsa, huh?
Yeah.
Well, I figured it would be Tulsa or Muskogee, yeah.
You saw him at the Berlin Festival this year, did you?

Yeah, he played there -- he played with -- Howard played with Dexter, Dexter Gordon group. Howard [Charles] and McPherson -- Stitt was supposed to be there, but Stitt didn't make it. Sonny didn't make it.
Where did you -- it says in here to tour Arizona and New Mexico with Eddie Hill. Did you go to Arizona with his band?
With Eddie's band?
: Yeah.
No, never did go to Arizona.
: No, you were in New Mexico.
New Mexico.
: Well, there's one thing. Where did Aaron Bell's mother come in the picture?
Aaron Bell's mother. That's what I was intending to get to when we first started talking. And that was -- now, you know, when I used to go to church?
: Yeah.
She used to play for the church choir.
: Yeah.
And oh, I used to get the biggest kick out of listening to her play. I enjoyed her playing. And you know, it's things like them that I think that have to wake me up about music.
: She was well-trained.

She was well-trained and could sing and his dad played trombone and his dad would play the trombone in the church along with her and the choir and then she also taught my sister piano lessons, see? And she was the one I really wanted to take lessons from, but the folks, you know, -- because I enjoyed her playing, you know.
: But you never did get lessons from her?
Never did get a chance to get lessons from her. But my sister did, see.
Yeah.

And that family -- that was some musical family, you know. He had -- Aaron had brothers and sisters -- he had a sister who played real good, real great. I don't know what she's doing now, what she did later. But I mean, she was there musically. Had a couple other brothers who was there musically.
Did you know him there?
Aaron?
Yes.

Yes. I used to cut Aaron's hair in school. You know, I was about 11th or 12th grade, see, when they'd send the younger kids over there to get their haircuts when we took barbering in school and Aaron would -- I'd always get him and I'd cut his hair and he'd just be tickling, laughing, "Hee, hee," and I never could give him a good haircut because he would laugh all the time I was cutting his hair.
(Laughter.)
We were talking about that at Michael's this past summer and he remembers it. That was so funny. Yes. But Aaron, he --
Well, Aaron was younger than you then.
Yes, yes. He was younger. See, now,
he was in grade school, see, when I was about my 11th grade, see. That's how they'd send the grade schools over for us to cut their hair.
Oh, I got you.
Yes.
So now, after Eddie Hill, then you -- then what happens next?

Well, after Eddie left, then we -- Howard, the group, you know, would continue to work around Albuquerque there and then long about that time, Gene Clay came through there and I'd never -- well, I never had heard a big band, you know, just to -- that was the first big band I heard in person and Gene ________ comes through there and they was doing 'Christopher Columbus' and I heard all that brass and the reeds and the rhythm section and oh, I like to went crazy, you know?
I hadn't heard nothing like that, you know.
That was a good band, was it?
It was a good band.
Were they playing a ballroom or something?

Actually -- let me see, there was Pete -- Pete was born in Muskogee, but he spent most time in Kansas City, you know, spent more time, you know, and -- but anyway, that was the first group that I took out and so then, you know, Walter Bales and we'd sit and talk and he says, "Well, I'll tell you what. I think you're going to have to make some changes. If I were you, I'd get a different guy on the trumpet," you know what I

mean, and he says, "Sounds like the drummer seems to be slowing the tempo down," you know what I mean. He says, "Now, I don't know nothing about this. So you just use your own judgment. I'm just --" we're setting talking, you know. He said, "But I'd like to see you get a good group." So I told him, "Well, everytime I make a change and make a better change, that's what I'll do."
So then I got Gus, [Johnson] Had not was supposed to have went with me on bass instead of Ramey, but Had not got a chance to go to Jeter - Pillars -- remember the Pillars in St. Louis?
In St. Louis, yeah.
At a club they worked so long, so many years.
And what was that, the Plantation?
That's it. That's it. And so Had not told me, he says, "Well, I know they offered me more money. I think what I should do is go down there and take that." So I says, "Well, everything's cool."
What was Gene Ramey doing --
He had been working with Countess Johnson. You remember Countess Johnson?
Oh, yes. Well, I don't know her, but I know of her.
Of her, yes. And she had had a group there and --
Was she a good piano player?

Yes, she could play. When Mary Lou got sick, they sent for her to play in Mary's place. Yes, she could handle a job, you know. I didn't enjoy -- I enjoyed her playing, but I didn't think she could really outplay Mary.
No, well, there weren't many people that could.
Right, that's the way I felt.
(Laughter.)
What about -- did she sing, this Countess Johnson, or was she just a piano player? (Unintelligible)? Or did she do like Julia Lee?
I don't think she did much singing, if any. Yeah, very little, if any. But she was a good pianist. And so --
Gene Ramey was with her?

Gene had been with her. But at this time, I got Gene, so that worked out good. And then I made a few changes and I got Willie Scott in the band. And let's see, Popeye left the band. After Popeye left the band, then I got Yardbird. So I had Yardbird --
Well, where did you hear him?
Well, the first time I heard Bird was when I was working out to the Monroe Inn with Hop

and I thought I had met most of the musicians in Kansas City, but I happened to be coming through the street on this particular night, you know, and you know how they would pipe the music outside? Cats be blowing in the mike? And you would hear it out in front?
Oh, loudspeaker over the door.

Loudspeaker. And so, I was walking across the street and I heard this sound. I said, "Oh, wait a minute. I haven't heard this cat before." So I decided to go in and see who it was. So I went in there and listened to him blow. After they finished playing, I walked up to him, said, "Hey, man, I haven't met you. I've met most of the cats, but where have you been?" He said, "Well, I've been down in Ozarks with George Lee's band. You know, it's hard to get musicians to go down to the Ozarks because it's so quiet down there. So I figured I wanted to do some woodshedding and so that's why I went." I said, "Well, man, you play different from anybody around Kansas City." He said, "Well, I've been down there woodshedding, you see. That's what's been happening." And that was our first meeting.
What year would this be? '37 or '38?

It's '37, '37, because he came to work with me in '38. See, he worked with the small group there for about four or five months and then he decided, he said, "Man, I want to go see New York. I'm just going up there. I want to

see it." And that's when he went -- you know, just went on a trip, stopped in Chicago and went on to New York and he was telling me about how he stood out there and looked at the sign that said Savoy Ballroom. He looked at the marquee and how thrilled he was. He told me about that after he came back. He said, "Man, that Savoy, just thrilled as I could be. Just standing there, looking at the marquee and just looking at everything," you know. And he came on back to Kansas City. He came back to Kansas City, he started working with Harlan Leonard's band. So he was working with Harlan's band and so by this time, you see, I've got a big band started.
But, Jay, was he hard to get along with when you had him in a small band?
No, no, no --
Was he reliable?
Well, now, I'll tell you. I think that's when he first got his first taste, you know.
Of the habit.
First taste of the habit.
Yeah.
When he was with the small band?
With the small band. But he was making time.
Yeah.
But the reason I say when he first
got his first taste, because sometimes you see him do this on the stand, you know.
Yeah.
So I think that's when he got his first -- but he went, came back, started with Harlan. So he'd evidently kicked it.
Oh, yeah.
He kicked it.
Yeah.
And we had a battle of the bands with Harlan Leonard one night -- was it a battle? Yeah.
Was this with your small band or --
The big band.
Oh.

See, and the big band, you know, and they can't be very old, and so Bird come up after we got through and said, 'Man, I want to play with you cats.' I said, 'Well, man, you know, you're with Harlan. You know Harlan ain't about to let you go.' He said, 'Well, man, I'll leave the band.' I said, 'Well, you got to give them some kind of notice or something.' He said, 'Well, okay, I'll give notice. I'll give him two week notice -- I'll give him a week.' I said, 'Give him two weeks' notice and take your time and come on in the band.' He said, 'Okay.' So he gave Harlan notice and come on with the big band, you know.

Now, during that time, see, that's the reason I say he had broke his habit, because he would take the reed, see, and I'd as point him, you know, to rehearse the reed section, because we would have section rehearsals. The brass would be over here rehearsing. The reeds would be over here. Bones over there, rhythm section over here, different parts of the hall, you know, whatever, you know. And then we'd bring the whole thing together, you know. And Bird used to keep right on and he'd keep right on them cats, you know.
He was really conscientious about it then?
He was conscientious about it. See, now, I never was worried about the reeds because I knew what Bird was going to do with them, you know.
Who was writing for you?
Well, Tadd Dameron was doing some writing. See, Tadd Dameron was hired to write for Harlan Leonard.
That's what I thought.

He was there with Harlan, writing for Harlan. But one day, Tadd brought one of his arrangements over and we played his arrangement and he said, 'Man, you all play this arrangement and make it sound like a different number. Harlan and them been playing this number all this time, but when you all play it, it's a different tune.'
: The Harlan Leonard band was pretty good, wasn't it?
It was good.
: Did he have -- what was that tenor player's name?
Bridges.
: And he had Beckett on trumpett.
Fred Beckett. But I think the difference was in the phrasing.
: Yeah.

See, that's what Tad meant. See, we actually phrased completely different from Harlan. See, Harlan and them was doing it (singing) quick phrasing. But we did that long phrasing. You know, if we -- if they had a bunch of notes to do, they did a bunch of notes. But they was phrasing long, you know, singing. That's what we --
: And it would swing that way.

Right. We always said sing. If you're playing a horn, make that horn sing. You know, yeah. Make it sing and that's why we laid on them first men so, because your first man, if he's singing and everybody is supposed to sing with him, you know, --
: Well, this is -- it's funny, we were playing -- what was it we were playing?
: (Inaudible).
Oh, some of Andy Kirk's old records. And Helen said that the trouble with that band was it didn't have a first man.
They didn't phrase right.
Thank you, thank you! That is -- that's it. It was a good band.
That's right.
And they were smooth.
That's right.
But their phrasing. See, the first man. See, now, just like when our first man -- now you know that was Charlie and J.J., as long as we had that music up there --
J.J. who?
John Jackson.
Oh, John Jackson, yeah, yeah.
As long as that music was up there, I had John phrasing. But when we did a head tune, Bird phrased.
(Laughter.)

See, Bird phrased, and Bird set most of the riffs, set most of the riffs. But all that head stuff, Bird did the phrasing. But on that stuff that we had to play down, J.J. phrased. And then, you see, it got to the point that Bird, sitting there with J.J., see, he got to the point where he was
playing them first parts just beautiful and he didn't have the tone J.J. had.
No, no.
See?
Well, that was the worst thing about it really.
(Laughter.)

Right. He didn't have a tone. But he had such a feeling. He had such a feeling. You know, I had some guys to argue with me. Oh, they thought I was crazy. They come up and ask me a question, they said, 'Well, what did you think about Bird's playing or this, that?' And we got to speaking, you know. So I said, 'Well, to cut a whole thing short, there's nobody's be-bop and there's this and that other and that other.' I said, 'Regardless of whatever he paid, Bird was the greatest blues player in the world.' And they thought I was crazy. They -- oh, they said, 'Man, you got to be out of your mind. What are you talking about? Bird was just plain old blues.' I said, 'Well, you better go back and listen.' Everything Bird played, if he played a sweet tune, it was the blues. 'If I Should Lose You --' (singing.)
(Laughter.)
All that stuff. Them slow tunes that he did, them slow pop tunes. Played the blues.
Yeah. But of course, the thing that
-- I guess the thing was that his tone sort of -- you know, like when Johnny Hodges plays the blues, now, that's a warm thing. But when Charlie plays it, it's an entirely different thing.
It's a different thing because what he's lacking in tone, he makes up on the other.
Yeah.

He makes up. And he can turn around and play 20 notes where Johnny played one note. But he made you like them 20 notes. When he got through with them 20 notes, he made you like it and he fall out of this.
Yeah.
Yeah.
Well, now, how much do you think he changed after the time he's with you? What happened to him in his music?
Bird's music?
Yeah, do you think he remained the same person or do you think he --

Bird was the same person when he played that big band. If anything, he lost after he got so far out. If I were -- here's what I mean. Bird was at his peak, he did his peak stuff -- I'll never forget. We played a one-nighter in Baltimore, Maryland. Bird was straight. And also a broadcast up there in Savoy Ballroom and he played

"Cherokee". The man, I think, must -- at the radio station must have been a musician because he said, "No, let's don't stop it. Just keep going." And we did. We kept it going right on through the night, you know what I mean?
(Laughter.)

Right on through the thing. He said, "No, don't stop playing no theme. Just keep going." And we just kept going. See, a lot of people thought that -- see, after Bird got so involved, that's what I'm trying to say, into the stuff, see --
Yeah, well, that's what I'm trying to -- what you think.
Bird was in his tops when he was with that band, with that big band of mine.
He was at the peak of his inspiration, but he was straight as well, so he was all set to (inaudible).

He was there and he played more -- and I still say I just wish that I had been -- had I had the money, had I ever had the money, because I would have made records of some of the stuff that we did and I don't know why I didn't get in touch with Mr. Bales and just tell him to pay for these sides and just keep them until I can see him.
Well, you couldn't tell the future.
That's right. Couldn't tell the future.
But I always wanted to do that. I tried to get Tomino to do that.
Tried to get what?
John [Tomino]
Oh.
Who was in Kansas City.
But Jay, when you started this band, you backed it. I mean, did you have enough money saved or did the Tominos -- I mean, you had to have money for uniforms and all. How did you do that?
But you're skipping something there, Stanley, because you haven't found out how come he let this small band go yet, you know? Jump from one to the other.

Okay, we'll start right there. Well, here's what happened with the small band. Dave Dexter begged me, he says, "Don't ever change this small band. Keep it like it is and let is stay right on through. Don't enlarge. Don't get no big band. Let everything stay like it is."
So I wanted to, but I also wanted to hear a big band. So when the job came along for the big band, I took the job. So I had to get more musicians.
What job was it?
That was at the Century Room and we started to work in the Century Room. So I had to have a bigger band at the Century Room and when I went up to Omaha and got Some
of Nat Towles' men
In fact, Mr. Bales gave me the money to do that, to go get these guys. But all other monies come right out of the band. A lot of people they think that Tomino didn't spend no money for that band.
He just booked?
That was all. All that money, everything, from the time we made 'Confessing the Blues,' that was the money that carried the band. That was the money.
Yeah.
It carried itself and a lot of people -- I've heard a lot of people say that the Tominos were spending money on the band but no, that was their own. That band carried itself.
Well, now, when you were talking about your father and big business like, now, when you get this big band, you sort of, being a good businessman --

No, I was worse, I got worse, because I was like this. If a guy says, 'Well, man, I see a horn I want.' If I had the money, I'd say, 'Well, can you do better? Can you do this? Get it.' I lost -- I liked the big band so well that I lost the value of money. I lost the value of money so that when I come out of the service, they told me, they says, 'Now you out of the service, but things have changed. Now, get you a small group and we'll get the same money for a small group you'll get for a big band.' 'No,' I says, 'I want the big
Well, I mean, you know, that -- you can look back now and see what -- but at that time, everybody was still thinking in terms of big bands, weren't they?
Right. But --
Well, you'd wanted to have a big band ever since you heard that guy, hadn't you?

You know, evidently that was the thing I think that really turned me around, when I heard all them trumpets, you know, and heard the saxaphone and trombones over here doing something else. That was it, you know.
All that force.

All of that. And then, not to speak of like when I first came to Kansas City, when I first came to Kansas City, I would go somewhere every night and listen because I would get off about 1:30 at night, and during that time, the joints was going until six, seven, eight, 9:00 in the morning, but the place I was working for, I got off at 1:30. So this give me a chance to make all the clubs, you know, and I used to come into clubs and I'd enjoy coming up and listening to Bus Moten's group, leave there and go hear another group, leave there and go hear another group, then go down on 12th Street and hear Pete Johnson play the blues and Joe Turner sing the blues. And Pete sitting there (tapping table) just for 20, 30 or 40 minutes, and just keeping a steady thing, steady roll,
steady rock and roll, steady beat. And Joe singing for 30 minutes. Well, I'd never seen anything like that in my life.
(Laughter.)

You know, it was exciting. It was exciting and -- it was exciting because I liked it, you know? You hear something you like and so I just never could get enough of it. I never wanted to go to sleep at night because I was afraid I would miss something, yeah.
Well, and also, you had quite a lot of big bands in Kansas City. I mean, you --
Right, never got a chance to hear big bands.
When did you first hear Mary?
Mary Williams?
Yeah.
Mary Lou? First time I heard Mary Lou, Andy Kirk played two nights, I think, a Friday and Saturday night out at the Fairyland Park (PHONETIC.)
Ferryland Park?
Ferryland Park, uh-huh.
Yeah.
And so when I heard they was going to be in town, I went out there that night.
You'd heard about Mary, had you?
How's that?
You had heard about Mary, had you?
Oh yes, I knew about here, reading about her in DownBeat and everything, you know.
Yeah.
And her records and so forth.
Yeah.

So I got a chance to go down here and hear her and when Basie came in town, I got a chance to catch Basie's group, you know, and when come in, I got a chance to hear their group. You know, big bands that came in, you know. And --
And what all guys were you listening to in Kansas City? Was Ben there then?
Ben Webster?
Yeah.
No, Ben was --
He'd gone.
Yes. During these times, I think Ben must have been playing with Ellington.
Yeah, I think so.
Uh-huh.
And Lester, of course, was with Basie.
And Lester was gone, you know. I never heard Lester, only when I heard him with Basie.
Is that right?
But so far as your band was concerned, who wrote the arrangements besides Tadd Dameron?
Well, Tadd was writing and Willy Scott.
Yes, he was the trumpet player, wasn't he?
Tenor sax.
Oh, yeah, yeah.
Tenor sax. And --
Hadn't he been with Harlan Leonard? Willy Scott?
No.
Well, what was the guy in Harlan Leonard's band? Who was the Scott in that band? Oh, well, never mind. (Inaudible).
Bridges played tenor with Harlan. Bridges and --
Where did Willy Scott come from?
Willy Scott was from Kansas City, Kansas.
Oh, yeah, uh-huh.
And he also played with Margaret Johnson's band, the same band that Raney was with, same girl.
Oh, yes.
He played with Margaret and Piggy played with Margaret's band.
Orville Minor.

Uh-huh, ORVILLE MINOR. And so I -- Scotty played with the small group until he went in the service and then after he went in the service, I replaced him, you know. He went in the service, oh, I guess he must have went in the service as early as '40, 1940.
Well, who sort of decided the style of your band?

Well, I'll tell you, the style was set this way. We did -- you know, we had a lot of music. But besides having a lot of music, we had twice that many head arrangements. Our style was set with head arrangements, with head arrangements, things that's done on the stand, at rehearsal, and the guys, they -- well, young. They could remember. They could remember. If we said, 'We're going to do it this way,' we did it that way.
They were relatively simple.
That's right.
Yeah.
And then -- it's just like we had numbers that could last ten, 15, 20, 30 minutes, the way we did them. One that last 30 minutes, we knew exactly what to do. We knew just --
Backgrounds behind the guys?
That's right.
(Inaudible).
We knew where we was going and we knew when we was going to get out of there, you know what I mean?
Yeah.

And that was the main thing. See, if we decided -- we start -- a lot of time, especially with rhythm section particularly, drum, bass, piano and guitar, we would just start. One chorus, second chorus, the cats want to come in, keep them out of the third chorus.
Probably setting them up.
Setting them up.
Yeah.
By the time we get to the fourth chorus, man, they raring to go, you know, they're raring to go, because see, we still trying to build, too.
Yes.
And by the time then we turn them in and I just give them that, they there.
Yes.

'Pee-Bo-Pent-Bo', (singing.) See, they ready to go, see. So then it was decided we're going to get in the bus, you know. 'Let's get in the bus.' Okay. Everybody starts setting it down. But everybody's got a job, see.
(Laughter.)

Bird going to set the riffs in the reed section, [Bob Gould] Buddy and Piggy going to set the riffs in the brass section, and when -- and the bones, you know what I mean. Sometimes got to have one bone, to have one bone, he'd have to go with the brass. If I had two bones, then they could work together. But they was -- either alternate, do it one way or the other. So consequently, we played so many head arrangements. That's where it was set. But we just sit and start playing, the rhythm section.
Now we had tunes that we would take on, tunes like "Willow, Weep for Me." We called that particular tune sport them up.
What?
"Willow Weep for Me," we called that "Sport Them Up."
Sport them up?
Sport. S-p-o-r-t, sport. "Sport Them Up."
(Inaudible).
Uh-huh. Now, the way we would do that, though, we was playing "Willow Weep for Me" though, see?
(Laughter.)
But nobody knew it. The guys would say, "What's the name of this?" Musicians. They'd say, "Sport Them Up."
(Laughter.)
But it was "Willow Weep for Me," see?
The chord foundation was the same.
Right. We would start and we playing the rhythm section, playing altogether, we're playing the same chords. But what we doing is not "Willow Weep."
No, no.
Uh-huh.
And the guys have got different riffs going.

Got different riffs. And then, like you say, when we go for that out chorus, we got three ways going. The bones going doing one thing, the reeds doing a thing, the brass doing one thing. Not clashing. That was the main thing. They never did clash. Because when you start clashing, you in trouble.
Well, everybody's getting into holes, I mean, so the brass (inaudible) hole there.
Right.
And the trombones are finding their own (inaudible).
Right, they got to find, you know.
Yeah, the pace.
So then, after playing so many heads together, they know how to find their hole where they belong.
That's what made it easy.
(Laughter.)
(Inaudible) whole thing.
Right. So actually, we got a format, but the format was formed and we didn't know it.
But it was --
Created it, as you went.
That's right.
Some of the written arrangements would be less in your style than really the heads were.
(Inaudible).
Well, I think that some of the arrangements that Tadd and people wrote were perhaps rather more formal and therefore they'd come out stiffer than the heads.
Well, that's true. But it was one thing that I did like about the guys, like you say, they would be formal, stiff arrangements, but when those cats got through with them --
Yeah, well, they got them really down.
When they got through with the arrangements, it was back to what we was doing.
Yes, yes.
You know, probably wasn't written that way. It wasn't written that way.
Oh, you mean they'd --
But we made it that way.
They adapted it to your style.
That's right.
(Laughter.)
Listen, Jay, how long was Bird with you in the big band? How long a period was that?
Bird was with the big band from the time he joined Harlan Leonard --
That's after he left Harlan and came with you, huh?
He stayed with the big band until -- I think I let Bird go in Detroit and that was 1940 -- about the last of '43, pert-near '44.
So how long would that have been? About --
So that had to be -- '40, '41, '42, '43, four years.
No kidding? No wonder you say he was blowing his best stuff then.
That's right. That was four years. See, and --
He really found himself in a big band right there.
That's right. And then the thing

about it, see, when Bird started getting into this other thing we was talking about, started getting into that, all he wanted to do was put his horn on his arm and just go down to Monroe's, Minton's, and just like I go in there and get me a taste, little couple of tunes, get off, come back in another hour and get a couple of tastes, go blow a tune. He didn't have his heart like it was with that big band.
No.
Because I remember one night, he told me just as plain, you know, when things would get tight --
Just one second, Jay. He must have left in '43 because he was with Earl in '43. That's what they all were saying, because of the record ban, they didn't make any records. He was with Earl.

Well, here's what. He left me in '43 and joined Earl. See, I let him go in the Paradise Theater in Detroit and then here's what happened. Andy Kirk was playing in town and Andy took him all the way back to New York. We was in New York two weeks. He got to New York a week before we did, Bird with Andy. So I run into Earl Hines. I'll show you something. Now, you don't know how to handle these guys. You don't know how to handle them. I'll take him and I'll make
a man out of him." I says, "Okay."
Three months later, I saw Earl Hines and Earl Hines was screaming to me, "Come and get this man. Get this man away from me. That's the worst man I've ever seen in my life."
(Laughter.)

"I've never seen anything go down like that. See, he owes everybody, every loan shark in town. Owes everybody over there at the Parlor Theater, owes everybody in the band. He's -- I bought him a brand new horn and he's so bad, --" you know.
What did you let him go for in Detroit?

And I kept wondering what the people was laughing about. He was in his stocking feet and his big toe was showing.
(Laughter.)

You didn't know it.
So I'm sitting over here at the piano

And so --

I mean, --

Arranger?
Huh?
An arranger?

-- use baton. Don would stand up and use the baton, you know.
Yeah.

Yeah.

Your book, I see.
Uh-huh. Yeah, we just played our book

Who said that?
Ramey, you know.
Oh, yeah.
Yeah, well, Ramey was always very close to him.

Yeah.

So when he went into -- so he went down in his books, well, when he did that, then I think that's when we -- we went heavy in the books. with that last tune, we fell right into him and that was one tune, that 30 minute tune, we played that 30 minute tune, we had the same reaction again, about 20 minutes they were just hollering and screaming for 20 minutes and Lucky couldn't go on.
What was the number you played.
We called it Roll 'Em.
That wasn't Mary Lou's Roll 'Em, was it.

No, no, that was our own Kansas City Roll 'Em and so that was it. And so then Lucky, he called me over, 'come here you old devil so and so' and he says, 'my God, listen,' he said 'I want you to go with me this morning,' and I said, 'okay, all right.' Well, Buchanan had been waiting, brought me up there once or twice for Lucky to meet. Lucky said I ain't got time, I'm leading the band. I'll catch you later on.

So Buchanan didn't have to bring me back because Lucky come over and got me and said you go with me this morning. He took me around the town and we had a few tastes, which was nice, but he told me, 'I'll tell you, man, you guys blew us out of there, did you know that?' I said, 'oh, no,' and he said, 'yes, yes, I got so carried away and excited and everything I fired three of my good men there.' He did fire three of them that night, of course, they knew he was going through that thing.

So it wasn't no stopping, I knew they wanted to go all the way.

Yes, the house bands.
The house bands and things like that, and then Gail had bands.

Yes. He booked us down in the theatres and different places, upstate, you know, and Jersey and up through that territory, and in fact, that was the first time that we did some dates, that was the first time we did some dates with what's his name, Don.

Mississippi --
Yes, and all that, so --

He didn't send no nothing, so we get back to New York, well, quite naturally we had to send back to them

for money and they had this bus that we had from Jersey, whatever it was that we had carrying the whole group, so when they called me down there, Gail told me, look, now, Jay, we're going to have to run into the loan company here, we are trying to run a business here, but I said look you all goofed us up, we just got completely goofed. You have nothing -- well, whoever was supposed to have sent that out, we didn't have anything to do with that, and that we feel that's not our fault.

I said, yeh, so they said, now, here's what we're going to have to do, we're going to have to get our money back that we put out on you and they had it right to the __now, we sent your money here and sent you there, money there and so on, says now we've got to get our money back. So now either that or we're going to have to take over a certain percentage of the band and everything, you know what I mean.
So in the meantime to me, though, he was with us --

Yes, he was traveling with us then.
Oh, he was.

Yes. So Tomino had realized what they was doing, you know what I mean, so after he realized what they were doing, he told me, well, I'm going to Chicago now, because they intend to annihilate us. We're going to get annihilated here, but they wanted --
They did that on purpose.

Well, yes, see we had to get Tomino out of there and then -- see, I'm the one that owe them the money. In other words, he's got to go and then for me to pay them back, you know what I mean, because they were selling Jay McShann.

I'll be back in town, so well, while I was waiting for Tomino to come in town, some buy who does booking around New York, I forget what his name was he came in there and talked to me earlier, see, about doing a date in Washington, so I told him, yes, I'll do that date in Washington, how much was it. I have forgotten what it was, but it was nice diggings, one of those good dates, so he says, well,

yeah, so we got together and the date, while I was waiting to see Moe Gail and them and he gave me a deposit -- he give me a deposit of about $250 see, so after he gave me the deposit, and then Moe Gail, asked me, what was so and so talking to you about. I said, well, I'm doing a date for him down in Washington and so on and so and so, and we got together on the date and so on, and Moe Gail said you don't need no money from him, take that check and give it back to him. You get it from us.

I said, that's all well and done, so they said okay, listen come on down and we'll talk again tomorrow, and I said okay, and in the meantime, Johnny Tomino gets back in town and he talks very loud -- do you remember Beryl Adams -- GMAC, I believe it was? And Beryl was booking with GMAC, so in the meantime while Tomino was gone and talked with Beryl, we got a call from Beryl, Beryl said I just booked you on the 40 one- nighters, about two or three days, I just booked you on 40 one- nighters already.

And starting such and such a date, so then when I talked to Gail and them, I told them I said, okay, if we don't have your money together, such and such a date, I forget how many days they gave me, I said then we'll have to get together and work on something, because I want to see you get your money, so we'll see what happens.
Okay. They knew there was no way for me to get this money, but I found out that Beryl had called and said you can
get this money, anytime you want this money, you pay them off, you got it, it's here and so I was happy about that.
So that's what you did.

Yes. What we did, I didn't have -- we started on these one-nighters and so he had his man, Ben Bart to meet us in Cincinnati, you know -- this is the date that the money is to be paid and so Ben Bart came up and said, well, man, be glad to have you with the fold and everything, he says, because I know, by God, there's no way you're going to get hold of -- I have forgotten how much it was, but that was my money then, this amount of money.

I said, well, I tell you what, Ben, it's been a pleasure, but I tell you what, I've got your check right here. He says, what. I says, yep, I've got your check right here. Right here it's all in full and I waited till the last night to give it to him. So he was telling me, we'll get ready and go back home, back into New York and I said, well, I tell you, got the check here so everything's all right, it's been a pleasure.
Well, Jay, was Ben Bart working for Moe Gale?
Yes, that was before he had got Universal.
Before Universal.
Yes. Oh, I tell you --
I bet old Charlie Buchanan nearly died, because he was always in the back of it all, wasn't he.

Yeah, Charlie Buchanan, well, you know, he was running the Savoy for them, you know what I mean. And Charlie Buchanan used to tickle me, he says now you got a good band, they like your band here, but it's the raggiest band I ever seen in my life.

I says, well, okay. I said, well, John, I tell you what you do. Now, look, of all the things that you do tonight, get that music and take it home with you tonight and keep it. He said, well, what about the band, don't you want the band to -- he says, 'we've got all these dates, ain't no need of missing this money. I can be sending you this money while you're in the service.'

He says, 'we're booked a year ahead.' I said, 'well, in that case, here's what we'll do. Go ahead on and if everybody in the band agrees, they want to go ahead on and finish these dates, finish the dates.' I said, 'but take that music home with you tonight.' Oh, no!
Which was the music.
How did they know? Who was it?

And I took it down there, they give you a sort of --
