No, they wouldn't have thrown me out. I'd have never went, with my feet.
Well, what happened. So you took this C out, and what happened? You took this chart or whatever he wrote down, and what happened then?

Oh, I took that down. And quite naturally, you've got a lot of eager beavers in the Army, in the service. And they said, oh, I can get it out of him, I can get this out of him, I can get that out of them. And if they can, if you don't know your rights, they'll push you, they'll make you kill yourself. They'll do that to you.

So this old boy, he (unintelligible) I heard him that morning. I was laying up in my barracks, I heard him. I'll get him, I'll get him. Well, the way I felt, I knew my feet couldn't handle it. But I was -- and I didn't have to go. But they didn't know I knew I didn't have to go, see. Over there in the barracks because the -- you know what I mean, the sergeants and all those people coming down to the CORPORAL. They didn't know that I knew.

But, see, I knew, because Doc told me. So this old boy come over there, and they got an act of grabbing your bed and throwing you out of bed and -- one of those little Army beds. Kick it over and turn it out. I always slept with my bayonet right at my head. I seen them coming, so just about the time he got ready to grab that bed, I fell out of there with

that bayonet so fast, he took out of there screaming, back to the quarters. He took out of there screaming, he tried to kill me. I told them, 'no, I didn't try to kill him.' I said, 'but I wasn't going to have him throw me on the floor.' And I told them, 'no, I didn't try to kill him.' He said, 'well, what were you doing with that bayonet in your hand?' I said, 'keep him from turning my bed over.' It was funny.
And one of the lieutenants came by, and he says, 'Mac, I told them don't go over and bother you, right in front of all of them.'
Did he?
He says, 'Mac, I told them to don't go over and bother you, to let you alone. And just kept walking.'

So I got -- that's the way I got them up off me. But they'd do things that -- unheard of things. I'll make this cat a soldier, I'll make him do this, I'll make him do that. But I didn't mind doing it if I could have handled it, but I knew my feet -- I knew they couldn't handle it.
But I do say this: My feet felt better with them Army shoes. I didn't realize it. It was a while before I realized it felt better with them Army shoes than they'd felt in my lifetime.
But you didn't tell them that.
No, I didn't tell them that.
But, Jay, how did you get your discharge?
How did it finally come through? Did the Doc work on it, or what?

Well, I'll tell you what. All of a sudden, they decided to give me 14 days furlough. So I told the sergeant, I says, I was over there at the officers club, I says, they're giving me 14 days for nothing. I haven't done anything. What would they be giving me 14 days for? He says, well, the Army don't give you 14 days for nothing.

So he say, you better go on and take them. I says, well, I thought maybe I'd just stay right here. He says, no, you're going to take them because they don't give you 14 days for nothing. So I went on and took my 14 days. But the funniest thing, when I came back after my furlough was over, I had to go in the hospital. I had hemorrhoids. And I went in the hospital, the day that I got in there, they said, oh, man, this guy got to be operated on.

So about the next day or two, they operated on me, and -- oh, about the time I was getting ready to get out of the hospital, they says, well, we got pretty good news. They think they're going to let you out. I guess I'd been in there almost a year. I says, what do you mean, let me out? Say, it looks real good, I heard your name come up with some other names over there.
I said, yeah? I said, -- so after I got out, I went down in my area, one of the lieutenants told me, he says, Mac,
why don't you just go on out. We're going to -- just go on out for the fun of it. He says, you're going to get out of the service, anyway. I said, no, I ain't taking no chances, I'll stay here.
I really wanted to go out and shoot with them that day. But I said, no, no, I ain't going to do it, I'm going to stay right here. But I got out of the service (inaudible).
Well, John, didn't you tell me that while you -- weren't you near L.A.?
How's that?
Weren't you near L.A. at this time, with the group you were with? Where were you?
When I was in the service?
Yeah.
I was in Georgia, Camp Stewart.
All the time?
Yes, Camp Stewart, Georgia. All the time until they sent me up to release me in Chicago. This -- Sheraton, right out of Chicago.
Oh, I was --
And you mean they just got around to that on their own? I guess there had been enough recommendations on your record or something on the feet, and then the hospitalization, huh?
Well, the doctor told them at the
beginning, he says, -- about how did I get in the service, and he says, it's a shame the way they send some of these guys up here. You ain't got no business up here.

But I didn't get out right away. But the time that -- but I think really, after they got a chance to study my case, after I had to go in for this operation, and while I'm in for a hemorrhoid operation, they said, let's see his record, and that's what rushed it. Otherwise, I'd have probably still been there even longer.
So they looked around and said, well, he's got flat feet, he's got allergies and --
But now when you get out you reform the band.

Well, yes. I'll tell you what I did. When I first got out, I came to Kansas City, and I was lucky enough to run into Dave Dexter, and he was going this thing with Capitol Records. And I think Julia was on there, and I backed her on a couple of tunes, Julia Lee, Tommy Douglas, Oliver Todd, and Baby Lovett and those guys.

And I happened to run into him that day. And so he says, well, come on down, and I'm recording these guys here, and so I got in on that record session. And he asked me what I was going to do, and I told him, -- I probably go back and try to put the band back together again. And so actually, what I did, I got a job back in New York and I went back there to
organize the band. And then -- oh, I had different people writing, you know what I mean. And --
What job did you get?
I was working there at 52nd Street at -- what club was that?
The Downbeat Club, I think.
I believe it was, right. Yeah. That was it.
Released and reformed band. Julian was resident at Downbeat Club in New York.
Right.
In June '46, he took own band to Los Angeles for residencies including Susie Q Club, Hobo Club. Then it goes on, during the '50s and '60s, Kansas City.
Yes.
Well, how long did you keep the big band?

Well, the big band didn't last too long because -- I'll tell you what, bythe time we got to the West Coast from New York, by the time we got to the West Coast, I had seen the handwriting. And so I got my check from Decca Records -- well, it was from Leeds Publishing. And so I don't know, I guess I must have gotten a $3,000 or $4,000 check.
So I got all the guys together in the group and told them, I says, well, fellows, this is the end of it. Because I
was losing money right and left, right and left. It cost me to play dates.

And so I told them, I'm going to send everybody home. And I'm just going to use a small group. So then I -- Witherspoon was with me then. And how I ran into Witherspoon, we did a one-nighter in Vallejo, California, after I'd came out of the service. I had Blues Bailey singing with me, but he went over to join Charlie Barnet . And so I didn't have a blues singer that night.
Who was that?

Blues Bailey. I'm trying to think of what was his first name. What was his first name? Max Bailey. Max "Blues" Bailey. And so he was supposed to join Charlie Barnet . And then I don't think he lasted over a few days with Charlie Barnet , because he had a pretty good drinking problem, and so Spoon was at the dance that night at Vallejo, California. So he says, hey, man, where's Brown? I told him - I'm trying to think, where was Brown then?

Well, Brown wasn't with the group. So I told him he wasn't with the group, and I -- he says, well, who you been having? I told him I'd been having Bailey and I told him Bailey was going with Barnet (inaudible). So, man, I think I can sing the blues. Let me do some blues with you. So he got up and sang some blues.
And he'd been tending bar or something, wsn't he?

I think so. He'd been doing something, I've forgotten. But he was just kind of fooling around. So I says, well, look, man, what about -- say, I got some old dates I got to do out here. They expect me to have a blues singer. What about finishing these dates? He says, yeah, I'm ready.
So he and I got together the next afternoon and we had a rehearsal with some things. And a few tunes, and some of these tunes he don't have to sing, you know what I mean.
Yeah, but when did you start singing yourself?
Well, I'll tell you when I started singing. I started singing -- I actually didn't start singing until I'd say about 1968.
Oh, I see.

See, I didn't do any singing -- well, because a lot of the jobs I was on, I got by, I didn't have to sing. Well, then, after about 1967, '68, I was getting all these jobs. Well, we've got to have a singer. Wasn't anybody going to sing. And there was a lot of places, 'they kept asking for the stuff that they knew me by.
Well, 'Cora Crossin' Blues, Hootie Blues,' won't you do none of them tunes? Well, that's what we remember you by. So I says, well, --
You almost get hung if you have a hit, don't you?

That's true, you do. And the thing about it is, it's like when Confessin' the Blues was a hit, sometimes you'd have to play that thing two and three times a night. I mean, the crowd was just raising cain. And things like this, things that had to happen.

So I realized, well, I'll just have to go ahead on and do it. So I just started doing it. I could have been singing before. But I always liked to have a good blues singer or whatever they sing, if they sing pop, a good pop singer or a good blues singer, it didn't make any difference, and I always liked -- I guess it was a big band thing in me that I had a time getting out. And then after I realized it, I says, well, somebody has got to sing, so then I started singing.
Well, listen, did that -- I did a thing with Jimmy Witherspoon last year here, in L.A. And he just -- he could not say enough for Jay McShann and so on.
Is that right?

He said he'd be tending bar, and you took him and you broke him in and he said, they were the best years of his life. And he said that guy -- oh, he couldn't say enough. How long did he work with you?
Well, let's see. I guess he must have been with me a couple of years.
Yeah, it sounded like it.
Who did you have at that little band on

Well, I had Benny Bailey. There was a guy that played saxophone, alto saxophone, what was his name? We called -- his nickname was Floating Moody. I cannot think of his last name. Because he was a big guy and he'd stand up and play, and he'd look like he was floating when he was playing. And so we just -- and we called him that name and it stayed. That's right today, if I saw him I'd call him Float. I can't tell you his real name.
So who else? Pete McShann came back with me then. Pete McShann, Witherspoon, Floating Moody, myself, and Addison Farmer on bass.
Oh, really?
Uh-huh.
So, now, how long did you keep this group together for?
Well, I kept that group together for, I'd say, -- well, Spoon had been with me before those other guys. But I guess I kept them together about a year.
But you --
Say, that is right, I kept them there about a year or maybe a little better, because Addison's brother came to work with the group, Art. And Art worked with the group.
And he --
After Benny Bailey left. He went with Diz. Benny Bailey joined Gillespie in Chicago. And I sent for Art Farmer.
Had Art been doing much work then?
Well, I think not much. He'd been hanging around on the West Coast, I think. And so we got Art and --
This is when you found out the difference between the way Benny Bailey was playing.
Yes, I really got a chance to see it, because it was a -- yes, it's a complete difference. One was technical and the other was more or less swinging.
Now, at this time you did make some records out there, didn't you? Isn't that when you made 'Slow Drag' or 'Buttermilk' and things like that?
Oh, yes, I did some things like that. Now, of course, that was during the time when the band was on, we just bootlegged.
Oh, you did?
Yes, yes.
Out here on the West Coast.
See, because the record ban was on.
Oh.
And --
So that would be '47.

Right. So this guy asks me, he says, well, look, he says, don't nobody know nothing about it. He says, you come on out and we'll go to a studio and one of these things. And at the same time, right around that time, is when I did 'Ain't Nobody's Business.'
With Witherspoon?

With Witherspoon. And then Witherspoon -- I couldn't -- let me see, well, I decided not to use my name because they were getting suspicious that I was doing some things. So as they was getting suspicious about me, then I'd say, you know, Spoon, I'll make this session, but let it be your session.
So it was Spoon's thing.
Oh, yeah, because it was safe for him, wasn't it?
Uh-huh. See, he was a singer.
Yeah.
He could get by.
Did any of these records sell well at that time?
Oh, 'Ain't' Nobody's Business sold all over the country.
Did it?
Yeah, that was a thing that put Spoon on the --
I was going to say, that was his first big hit.
That put Spoon on top.
But did you get any benefit from those sales?
No.
But Witherspoon did.
Yeah. I just told him, listen, take the whole thing.
That's what happened.
If it had been under your name, you might have. But you might have been in trouble.
That's true, see, so I to avoid that I just told him, just go ahead, Spoon, and whatever -- you all go ahead. You all pay me what I get paid for a session, and that's it.
Well, how long did you stay out on the coast that time?

Well, I stayed out -- I was out on the coast, I guess, about maybe a year and a half, and then the band went off. Then when the recording ban went off, well, then, most of the time that's what I was doing, recording behind other people, out there.
Who, for instance?
Oh, let's see, I think I -- who all did
I record behind? I think I did another session behind Spoon. They had some blues guy up there, what was his name?
(Inaudible.)
Not Johnny Lee Hooker, but the other guy.
(Inaudible.)
Oh, what's the guy that T-Bone did all the battles with?
Roy Brown.
No, no, the crazy guy.
Oh, you mean Joe Turner?
No.
Fulsom?
No, no, no. You know, the difficult guy that T-bone --
Oh, Wynonie Harris.
Wynonie.
Oh, Wynonie?
It wasn't Wynonie?
No, it wasn't Wynonie. But this guy, he had bad meter, and then --
Oh, so he was more oldtime, was he, then?
Yes, and a lot of them -- I was just -- the studio would call me, and a lot of people that I don't even remember that I played behind.
Yeah.
A lot of names.
What labels were they?
Let's see, it was Downbeat label, Marvin -- do you remember Modern Records?
(Inaudible.)
And they had about four or five other labels that came up that you didn't hear anything.
You don't mean PeeWee Craton, do you?
No, no, I remember PeeWee. No, it wasn't PeeWee.
(Inaudible) Amos Milburn.
How's that?
Amos Milburn?

Yeah, I remember, Amos was out there. Yeah, I remember Amos. But I didn't back him up. But it was a lot of people that the names never did do anything, because I was just sort of working with the studio. They'd call me --
House bids.
Yes.
Well, what were you doing with the night time? Were you working in clubs?
Well, I was doing pretty good, just recording. So I was just having a ball just recording, and they would pay me double. And they'd pay me double so I didn't do anything but record.
Did they use your name then, every time?
Well, no, I don't think so. Unless they had it in little print or something like that. So -- then I ran into Art while I was out there. Art Tatum.
Oh, yes. Tell us about that.

And we used to get together, and Art, he always liked to go to these after-hour places. And because this same guy down at Downbeat wanted Art to do a session for him, and Art was going to do a session for him, but I've forgotten -- they didn't get together on the bread. And Art said, well, I don't think I'll fool with it.

But Art and I was hanging out, we'd make these after-hour spots, and you know how Art is, he hates to go home. Art will hate to go home, so a lot of times I would be driving for him. So I said, Art, man, it's 4:00 in the morning, they're going to shoot us. Aw, that's all right, that's all right, it's early yet.
So sometimes we'd get home 5:00 or 6:00 in the morning. So I parked the car and get Art to the front door and say, see you later, take off.
Why, did his wife give you --?
Yeah, God knows, she'd be giving me the devil. So I would take off, and so he was -- he was -- once he'd get out, it was hard to get him in. Because he liked to sit around and play the blues.
Well, then he started you playing the blues.

Yes, well, he'd have me to start playing the blues. We'd be setting up tastes, oh, play the blues. Okay. I'd go and play the blues. And after a while, Art Tatum would come in. I'd just slide on out the piano stool and sit down. And you wouldn't have to ask him to play anything. A lot of people would make the mistake -- it's likely to be four, five, six or seven people in the room, and maybe somebody's high, Art, play so and so and so and so. That'd kill the spirit. It would -- he couldn't stand for nobody to ask him to play nothing.
I see. He just wanted to play what he felt like.
He just wanted to sit down and if he didn't do nothing but run over that piano for two or three minutes when he first sat down, that's what he -- he didn't want nobody to ask him.

But if they let him alone, he's going to play everything there is to be played, anyway. If they let him alone. You'd have to tell people, please don't. When he decides to play, he's ready to play. He's ready.
Would he like to have a drummer in back of him, or no?
Art?
Yeah.
Never needed a drummer, never needed nothing. Art Tatum, he never needed anything but Art Tatum.
Yeah. I just wondered, did it bother him if he had a drummer?

It didn't bother him at all. It might bother the drummer. The drummer or whoever else is there, because he did so many things, you know what I mean. It just -- that just made the drummer out of concept with what was happening. Basie or whoever else was sitting in there, the whole thing was out of concept.
And he didn't need anything. Of course,he knew that.
But these records -- I think you said that he liked to play the blues and did play the blues.
Yes, Art liked to play the blues. He would play them and sing them.
Oh, really?
Art used to play -- he would play and sing the blues. And he loved the blues.
Yeah.
Art Tatum loved the blues. When -- but, yes, he would play and sing the blues.
(Inaudible) nobody ever got up to do that on a record. I never heard him sing anything.
Yes, he would. But you had to catch him --
Yeah, when he feels like it himself.
That's right, when he feels himself, when he feels like he wants to do it. Yeah, you got to catch it. And he was just phenomenal.
Well, what happened after this spell on the coast? What did you do next?

Oh, well, what happened, while I was out there on the coast, my -- I was married to a girl in South Bend, Indiana, and we'd had our first kid. And I had never seen the kid. And so the kid took sick and she sent me a wire and called out there and said, oh, she turned blue, we think she's dying and this and all.

So I wired her, I said, well, I'll be in. And so I drove back. And so in the meantime, by the time I get back to South Bend, the kid's all right, well and hearty and everything. It was just one of those things that they got excited about.
That was lucky.

Uh-huh, and so I'm back in South Bend now. See, otherwise, I wouldn't have left the coast, because I had some things that I wanted to do. But after leaving the coast I went back to Chicago, I said, well, I'm back here now. It was only about 90 miles out of Chicago, South Bend. And so I started doing a few gigs around there.
And then at that time, I ran into a guy named -- well, Jesse Price and Shep, the bass player.
Oh, Ernie Shepherd.
Yeah, and they were with their --
Oh, Slim.

Slim Gaillard, yes. And they -- Slim fired him in Chicago, so he fired him in Chicago, then we got together. He got fired, so then we got together and started doing some dates around Chicago. Go up to Milwaukee and Michigan and just all right around in there.
So I did those dates, dates like those, up until they wanted us to go south. And I went down south, Memphis and through Mississippi, all down through there.
The three of you?
No, well, I had a couple of horns and Jack Cooley, who was singing the blues then.
Who?
Jack Cooley. And --
Who was booking you then?
I just did it myself.
Oh, you did?

Then I knew certain guys in certain areas like -- oh, in Memphis, I knew Henry Jones, and I told Henry, well, Henry, how many dates can you handle, and Ralph Weinberg, I knew him, in Virginia. He used to do all those dates with the band in Virginia. And we'd tape maybe eight or ten dates. Then I'd tell Henry to contact a cat over in the

next state, so he'd go on over there and maybe set up over to Georgia or somewhere, some dates over there. Then he'd contact the guys in Florida. Used to have a two-spot, and they'd set up a few dates. So we made -- the last day of the tour, we stopped in Wichita, Kansas. So I told the fellows, well, fellows, I'm going on into Kansas City, and we just shut the group off, sent everybody home.
And I went into Kansas City because the kids are getting up now.
You've got two by now.
Yeah, I got two now, yes.
Was the first one a boy?
No, all three girls. Only got three and all three of them girls. So I knew that I would have to settle somewhere, because the oldest --
Just one thing. Where did you do those records with Priscilla Bowman?
That was 1955.
That was in Chicago.
That was in Chicago, yes.
Well, where did she come from?
She came from Kansas City, Kansas.
Oh, yeah?
Uh-huh.
Well, you had quite a hit with her, didn't
Yes, yes.
'Hands Off.'

'Hands Off,' yes, it was, yes. And in fact, that was the first time I had went out on the road, since coming to Kansas City in 1951. I came to Kansas City the year of the flood in '51, and then I decided, I said, well, I better get a place here, because the kids will have to go to school somewhere. And so I just sort of went back and settled in Kansas City. And after the kids got of age, about four or five, then she started school and then I ran into Priscilla and we did this Hands Off thing, and '55 I went on the road, stayed off and on about a year, til it died down, til the record died down.

In fact, Ben Bart booked us on that. And then I came on back into Kansas City, because I would get on those jobs and stay there four, five years. Because when I went back in '51 I stayed there until '55 on that job.
What one job?

This was with the Johnny Bakers. And then after I went on the road off and on for about a year, I came back and went on another job, stayed about a year, like that, different jobs like that, up until --
These jobs were with a trio or what?
Well, I was using about six pieces.
Oh.
Uh-huh.
And you could stay in one place about a year with them?
Uh-huh. In fact, those six pieces stayed there for almost five years there, from '51 to '55.
Where did you play there?
That was the Johnny Bakers, in Kansas City.
Yes. Well, who did you have in that group?
Well, I had Piggy Minor on drums; Al Duncan guitar player named Gene Griddins; and Fats Dennis. And had a little girl, I used a girl, you know what I mean, girl singer.
What happened to that Priscilla Bowman?
She's in Kansas City now.
Does she not work?
Well, she went on the boat with me. Remember when we went on the boat down to New Orleans, what do they call it, the Delta Queen?
Oh, yeah?

Yes, the University of Nebraska sponsored a thing, for the Delta Queen to come up the Mississippi from New Orleans all the way up to Cincinnati. About a two week tour, and I used a girl on that. She was on that with me.
When?
That was in March.
Oh, you did?
Yes, right after my thing -- you remember, we talked about --
(Inaudible.)
Really? Well, it was May, really, because it was May when we made the trip.
Well, what sort of a looking girl is she?
I guess she's probably about five feet four, and a kind of brownskinned looking gal. Reddish light --
How old was she?
Well, she's about 50 now.
Oh, I see.
She's got to be 50 now.
Yes, I see.

And she was on that with me. She doesn't work regular. When they want a girl singer, I usually use her. And they wanted a girl singer on the boat, because they were showing the old days of the riverboat, old days, with everything coming up the river. And we'd stop in Natchez and did a show in Natchez and stopped in the other towns and did it.
And it took two weeks?
Yes, see, it was so slow coming up that stream, that --
That was in March of this year.
That was this year. May.
(Inaudible) in Kansas City.
I don't know anything about that.
We talked about it. I think -- in fact, there might be something in one of these books about it.
You ought to have gotten some publicity out of that.
Uh-huh, yeah. I know that -- oh, we stopped the show in Paducah, through Memphis, Louisville and to Cincinnati.
When did you go to New York the first time?
The very first time I went to New York?
Yeah, to Europe.
Oh, to Europe. I'm sure that was 1969.
That was with who?
Me, Eddie Cleanhead Vincent, Gene Ramey and Paul Gunther, and that was it.
And who did you go for that time?
(Inaudible.) Black & Blue.
Oh, Stanley, I know what I wanted to ask Jay. You did make a record with T-Bone Walker, didn't you, then?
That is true, we sure did. Yes, T-Bone was in Paris at the time. And T-Bone was -- he was tasting

pretty good. He was tasting pretty heavy. And that's -- he was sick then. I could tell it. And I hated to -- we wanted to do the session a lot of different ways, but I told the guys, let him alone, just let him -- don't let him alone, because I realize he was sick, see.

He wouldn't eat anything, he was just fighting that -- I believe it was vodka. Either vodka or gin. And then when he came back over here, he didn't last very long. He came back to this country, and it wasn't very long before he -- you know.
Well, his ulcers and everything were --
That's true, yes, yes.
Wasn't a bad record, though, Jay.
No, that's -- he and Hal Singer -- I think Hal Singer was on that record.
Yeah.
And you know how you take two guys that's strong-headed, and they was both strong-headed. And I told Hal, let him alone, you know what I mean. Let him have it, don't argue with him. And --
Yeah, it's a shame, isn't it?
Yes.
But since then, how many times have you been to Europe?
Well, about every year since, and sometimes twice.
So you're probably as popular there as you are here.
Well, better, I'd say.
Well, I think that last engagement at -- let's see, what was it that he did in Michael's Pub with the last time you were there? You brought in all sorts of people, didn't you?
Oh, the last time we were there. Oh, we had --
Jimmy Maxwell.
Jimmy Maxwell on trumpet, and Joe Morello on drums, Jack Six, bass, and a man with Duke, tenor man, Harold Ashby.
Yeah, yeah.
And -- yes, that was it.
Because you had recorded with Ashby in Chicago, hadn't you?
You see, --
So now, we're more or less up to date.
(End of Side One.)
-- in '78, you've got the keys to the city in Kansas City.
That's right, yes. We did a thing there at the Muhlbach, they called it. My day, day for Jay McShann, and they gave me the keys to the city. Had a nice
turnout.
And you had a special band, didn't you?
Yes, we had Buddy Tate, Cat Anderson, Gene Ramey, Gus Johnson, the old rhythm section.
Claude Williams.
Claude Williams.
When did you first work with Claude Williams?
Well, truthfully, the first time I worked with Claude Williams, it was about 1969 or 1970.
I wondered about that. So you hadn't worked with him earlier.

No, no, we had never worked together. I knew him, because I used to hear the guys talk about him as a musician. And I met him when I first came to Kansas City. But I had -- we had never worked together.
But since then you've been thrown together several times.
Yes, we've been together on a few occasions, yes. In fact, I didn't -- I really never knew -- didn't know that Claude was from Muskogee and he didn't -- I guess he didn't know I was from Muskogee.
There's one thing about Kansas City. There is much happening there, really, in terms of jazz, is there?
That's true.
When I was there, I thought, how dull at the Muhlbach, which has conventions and everything. You'd think they would have a group there all the time.

Well, you know, it's a funny thing. People come into Kansas City, and there's a lot of people asking, well, where's the jazz? But Kansas City doesn't have that much jazz. Now, Betty & Milt was there for awhile. They had a group, a duo.
Who?
Milt Able and Betty Miller. They -- Betty -- yeah, they were a married couple.
Oh, yeah.
But --
Well, you'd think a city that size could --

Yes, you would think they would. But they have been trying to get something started now at the Muhlbach, because Bud Johnson was down there not too long ago, and Raymond was there and he worked about four weeks there or five weeks, the different ones they brought in.

And I worked one week, and Raymond and Gus was there. Raymond and Gus was there about three weeks. They were there with Budd and another group, and they were there with me. Then Bud came in after I did and Gus didn't stay with Budd, but Raymond made a date with Budd, and I don't know who else followed in that.

But they've been bringing groups in there now, you know what I mean, and -- but, as you say, it's really been scarce for jazz in Kansas City. There's a lot of people that come in town, especially because they say, we heard a lot about Kansas City jazz, we want to know where the jazz is. But then there's no jazz there.
Well, it's too bad.
Jay, to finish this up. There's one or two things I think we've forgotten. One, the period when you sent yourself back to school.

Oh, yes. Well, what happened, I knew that my kids were getting up in age, and they was going to have to go to school somewhere, so that's why I decided to go to Kansas City. So I figured while they're in school, then I would go to school. So I went to the Conservatory.
The Conservatory of Music?
Yes, the Kansas City Conservatory of Music. And then we --
How big a place is that?

Well, it's affiliated with the University of Missouri in Kansas City. But at the time I went, they didn't have all these credits that they have now. But it was still a good music school. And I wanted to find out what I was doing, and -- because I'd played all those years and didn't know what I was doing. At least, if someone asked you, you
could tell them what you did. So I felt like I should learn that much of it, and then I would want to be able to read. And so that was --
Well, what actually did they teach you? What were the different --

Well, there were a lot of subjects we took. We took harmony, took composition, dictation, ear training, score reading, sight reading, and all -- and other phases of it, even music history and all that.
Oh, well, you found it very interesting.

Yes, it was interesting, because there was a lot of phases that -- certain phases that you liked better than other phases of the music. And so that kept it interesting for the courses that you didn't like too well.
Were there any particular composers that you did get to like? Well, Mozart, for instance, or Chopin. Were there any ones particularly, any studies you had that you liked?

Well, truthfully, Bach was quite a guy, there's no question about it. But I liked him for what he did, and I liked some of the others. Like you say, Mozart, Chopin, a lot of those guys for what they did. Because everybody had a story to tell, and it reflected in there what they were doing. In their works, and that was the outlook that I had upon it. In other words, say, for instance, if I'm going to
play Bach, I don't want it to sound like Mozart or Beethoven. I want to know that I'm playing Bach.

So I had respect for all of them. But, really, I never did put myself -- have any preference. It was just a matter that there were certain things that I wanted to do musically, and I wanted to get that done.
And there was a story you told me about one of the teachers overheard you practicing some of your own things.
Oh, yes, that was Dr. Bubendorff, and he --
How do you spell his name?
Dr. Bubendorff. He was a staunch German teacher.
How do you spell it?

B-o-u-b-e-n-d-o-r-f. Boubendorf. And he was real strict in his teaching. You might say, oh, well, -- like, phrases that we would use, and he'd straighten you out right quick. No, that's so-and-so. You don't call that a this or this, you call that so-and-so. He was very, very, very staunch and strict in his explanation, which was right. It's just so easy, because when I was being careless, just like I was playing along, or like I had been doing, I always thought D sharp and E flat was the same thing. Well, it is harmonically the same sound, but it's not the same thing.
And I had to go through all of that bag, you know what I mean, and get it straightened out. So it was a lot of fun and challenging.
But when he hears you playing your own stuff, didn't he have you play for the students?

Oh, yes, well, he heard me downstairs, I'd practice my lesson awhile, then I'd go off into some of my stuff. And so he'd stop by and listen. So he came in and told me, he says, listen, I want you to play this same thing in class such-and-such a day. And I didn't want to do it. I said, oh, no, no. And he says, no, that's what I want you to do. I want you to play this in class.
And then he would elaborate on it.
Oh, he'd discuss it.

And he'd discuss about the big bands and arrangements that he had heard by big band members and things, that he enjoyed. It was a surprising thing. After he began to see the other side as well as where he had been, the accomplishments and things that was being done. And then, of course, during this time they were trying to get this transition thing together, you know what I mean, together, because --
The Third Stream.
Yes, right.
So he wasn't sort of narrow-minded.
No, he was not narrow at all, and the
thing about it, he was so open-minded about everything. And then to hear a guy like that, Dr. Boubendorf, well, you expect him to be one way and that's it. But he was flexible.
The other thing we didn't mention was this film which you made in Kansas City.

Oh, yes. We -- Bruce Ricker decided he wanted to do a film on Kansas City jazz. And then as things rocked along, he wound up calling it 'The Last of the Blue Devils.' That's what he called the film. And, well, we had a big band and we had other smaller groups that also appeared. Basie came down, he talked, and then he got some -- oh, some -- Basie and them were doing some things, too, you know what I mean, which was Kansas City jazz.
Yeah, it was supposed to be a sort of Kansas City jazz thing.
Uh-huh.
Where was the -- what was the name of the place where it was filmed?

Well, this was originally filmed there at the Musicians Foundation. Now, that used to be the old 627 Local. And now that the -- they have merged, 627 and 34, the 627 union kept the old building, and they keep it for guys to come around, and they sit around and talk and maybe have a few sessions and things like that.
So they kept the building and -- after the merger.
And I understand that he's finally got the money to finish the job off.
Well, that sounds really good. I'm glad to hear that.
Yes, well, you did a lot of work on that. They've got to clean it up.

Yes. Well, actually, I think he ran into some difficulties along the way, because there were so many other things that he wanted to put into the film, and other musicians which really deserve to have been in there. And then it got to be a money problem, because --
It costs so darn much to edit that stuff.
That's right.
But he says he's got it now.
Oh, that's beautiful.
So maybe we'll see it next year.
Look forward.
All right. Well, thank you, Jay.
(End of proceedings as recorded.)

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Smithsonian opening notices and interview header
segments.summary: Copyright notice and title pages for the 1978 Smithsonian Jazz Oral History interview by Stanley and Helen Dance.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Birth in Muskogee and growing up with three sisters
segments.summary: McShann gives his birth date, January 12, 1916, and says he was the only boy among four children, outnumbered by his three older sisters.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Musical parents and his father's furniture-store job
segments.summary: His mother played church songs on piano and his father knew one tune; the family was poor. His father drove a truck for Ferguson Brothers Furniture for about 25 years.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: What and where Muskogee was
segments.summary: He describes Muskogee as a town of about 30,000 with several railroads, roughly 300 miles from Kansas City and 60 miles from Tulsa.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Grandmother, Indian Territory and the missed land claim
segments.summary: His maternal grandmother came to Indian Territory via Alabama and Texas, missed signing up for land by going back to Texas; his father's family came from Mississippi.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: His mother's name and talk of Indian ancestry among musicians
segments.summary: He gives his mother's name, Leona McBee, and the Dances discuss Indian blood in Ellington, Blanton and Pettiford and a possible Indian contribution to jazz.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Alligator and the rough club in Ponca City
segments.summary: McShann tells of the club in Ponca City, Oklahoma where Indians, whites and blacks mixed and a bouncer called Alligator cleared the room when fights broke out.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Whether Indians and liquor mix badly
segments.summary: He argues that holding liquor depends on the person, not on race, though Indians had reason to feel desperate given their situation.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Lowell Fulson and musicians who hid Indian blood
segments.summary: Asked about Lowell Fulson, he says many musicians had Indian ancestry and some hid it, while Mildred Bailey and Jack Teagarden admitted theirs.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Dizzy Green and others who passed for white
segments.summary: He tells how his school friend Orville Green went to Hollywood and passed for white, snubbing a friend, and mentions Willie Smith who could have passed.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Segregation on the road and the white trumpeter at the filling station
segments.summary: Prompted by Earl Warren's stories, he tells how a white trumpet player in his band was sent to the colored restroom at a southern gas station.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Stanley Dance's South America story and talk of Jim Crow laws
segments.summary: Stanley recalls being refused boarding in Brazil with Ellington's band because he was white; McShann and Stanley agree such laws were a hangover from slavery.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Sisters' piano lessons, the graphophone and forbidden blues records
segments.summary: He tagged along to his sisters' lessons, loved the family graphophone and hid Bessie Smith records his churchgoing parents wanted to get rid of.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: School singing with Miss Clark and no instrument
segments.summary: Elsie Clark taught songs by ear at school, and when a band instructor arrived his parents could not afford an instrument for him.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Teaching his sister's piano piece and picking out tunes
segments.summary: He showed his sister a piece at her lesson; the teacher told his mother he was getting free lessons, but there was no money, so he taught himself by ear at about ten.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Playing Backwater Blues at the school assembly
segments.summary: Pushed by the music teacher to play at a school assembly, he played Bessie Smith's Backwater Blues; students cheered but teachers and the principal disapproved.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Church songs and faking sickness to play the piano
segments.summary: He played church music at Sunday school and feigned illness to play the piano at home alone until a neighbor gave him away; his grandmother let him play other music.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Why they called blues and ragtime 'reels'
segments.summary: Asked about the word, he explains that blues and ragtime were all called 'reels' and meant bad music in his family's day.

segments.chapter: Childhood, family and learning music
segments.title: Manual Training High School and Mr. Collins's little band
segments.summary: He finished high school at 16, read widely, and Mr. Collins formed a school band with him on piano, rehearsing at his house; they played Christmas dates for about 80 cents a day.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Scholarship to Knoxville College and the stop at Fisk
segments.summary: He and Jesse Culbertson got scholarships to Knoxville College in Tennessee and rode with Culbertson's uncle to Nashville, where his old teacher urged them to stay at Fisk.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: No jobs in Nashville and playing a party for 80 cents
segments.summary: With no jobs coming through the Fisk office, he tried football, then played one or two songs all night at a school party for 80 cents before they were told to go.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Riding freight trains back to Oklahoma
segments.summary: Broke, they rode freights from Nashville to Knoxville and back, dodging railway agents who shot at them, until an old landlady fed them and sent them home.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Arriving home covered in soot and leaving for Tulsa
segments.summary: He came home as a 'tramp' to his sisters' mockery, then after a few days left for Tulsa to stay with an uncle and look for work during the Depression.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Sitting in with Al Dennie's band in Tulsa
segments.summary: Following the sound of a band rehearsing, he volunteered as pianist for Al Dennie's 12-piece band, who thought he could read and fake.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Repertoire with Al Dennie and checking details of the early years
segments.summary: Asked what he played, he says stock arrangements and tunes like Honeysuckle Rose, playing chords by ear; the Dances check spellings and the length of his stays.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Lee Deere, the Gray Brothers and Art Bronson
segments.summary: Lee Deere came to Tulsa to collect the Gray Brothers' group for his Kansas clubs; McShann lists the players and mentions Art Bronson's Denver band.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Lee Deere's $14 offer and leaving his aunt's house
segments.summary: Deere offered him $14 a week to play piano in Arkansas City, Kansas, and he left in a car before his strict aunt could phone his parents.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Essie Henderson, money tunes and Lee Deere's later career
segments.summary: In Arkansas City he learned old tunes from guitarist Essie Henderson, including 'money tunes' that gamblers tipped for; Deere later owned the Thunderbird in Las Vegas.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Playing duo with guitar and the Burton Brothers' club
segments.summary: Playing with just a guitar taught him a lot about filling in; he names the Cedars Club, also called the Burton Brothers Club, run by Clyde and Babe Burton.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Arkansas City as a bootleg town and the staged raids
segments.summary: He describes Arkansas City, Kansas, drawing patrons from dry Oklahoma and Kansas, and how raids were tipped off in advance and soon forgotten.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Four Roses and his first bad experiences with liquor
segments.summary: A non-drinker, he took a pint of Four Roses to a party and got sick; he recalls a similar first episode in high school and his father's mild advice.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Tobacco, cigars and chewing tobacco
segments.summary: Stanley's cigarette story leads to McShann's own sickness from chewing tobacco and cigars bought from the grocery store where he worked.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Calling his grandmother 'Mammy' and her snuff dipping
segments.summary: He tells how he called his grandmother Mammy to get cakes from her, and tactfully told her about the snuff running down her mouth.

segments.chapter: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
segments.title: Junior college in Arkansas City
segments.summary: With savings he enrolled in junior college in Arkansas City but money ran short when the clubs closed, though he sometimes played for Alligator in Ponca City.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Raiding the landlady's icebox and the call from Eddie Hill
segments.summary: Broke, he raided his landlady's icebox until she told him her son played in Eddie Hill's band in Shawnee, and he got a ticket and $3.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Eddie Hill and his Bostonians at the Bluebird Ballroom
segments.summary: He joined trumpeter Eddie Hill's eight-piece band at Shawnee's Bluebird Ballroom, with the Gray Brothers and Lester Taylor; Hill and Taylor wrote arrangements.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Silvas Resort in the mountains and not learning to read music
segments.summary: The band worked at Silvas Resort east of Albuquerque; McShann says he never learned to read because piano's two clefs seemed a chore and he wanted a horn.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Asthma, mountain air and smoky rooms
segments.summary: The mountain air relieved his childhood asthma, which has recently returned; he blames sinus, allergies and years in smoky clubs.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: The resort owner's quarrels and the Phoenix offer
segments.summary: The older white owner and his young wife fought, he was put out, and he offered the band a Phoenix job; Eddie Hill, apparently involved with the wife, would not go.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: The shooting at the resort
segments.summary: The owner caught Eddie Hill in bed with his wife, shot her and himself, and Hill fled up the mountain and returned in worn-out shoes.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Aftermath: the missing money and the owner's suicide
segments.summary: The commissioner offered the band work and got Hill out of town; the wife's mother and father also died, and McShann reasons the guitarist took the missing money.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Working for the Albuquerque commissioner and Howard McGhee
segments.summary: The band worked for the county commissioner's club, where trumpeter Howard McGhee joined them; they talk of McGhee at the Berlin festival and check the Arizona claim.

segments.chapter: Eddie Hill and Albuquerque
segments.title: Aaron Bell's mother and cutting Aaron's hair
segments.summary: He explains how Aaron Bell's well-trained mother played in his church and taught his sister, and recalls cutting young Aaron's hair in barbering class.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: First big band heard in person, with Junior Raglin and Maxwell Davis
segments.summary: In Albuquerque he heard Gene Coy's big band, his first, with Junior 'Bear Tracks' Raglin, blues singer Blues Bailey and Maxwell Davis, and was overwhelmed.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Hearing Jimmy Rushing sing a waltz, probably with the Blue Devils
segments.summary: He recalls a band with Jimmy Rushing singing 'When the Leaves Bid the Trees Goodbye', and he and Stanley conclude it was probably the original Blue Devils, not Moten.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Date of 1936, plans that fell through, and heading for Omaha
segments.summary: The big band was 1936; plans to join a Seattle group fell through, his father died, and he set off for an uncle in Omaha.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Tape change at sides 3-4
segments.summary: Header for sides 3-4 and brief talk about how long the transcript will take.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: His father's advice to make music a business
segments.summary: His father told him to treat music as a business rather than fun, a worry rooted in his struggles to collect money on his newspaper route.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Walking everywhere, feeding the hogs and curing pork
segments.summary: He recalls walking miles each day, carrying feed to his uncle's hogs, and the family curing pork in the wash house.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: The Jersey cow in the graveyard and Earl Hines's funeral-home story
segments.summary: Taking a shortcut by the graveyard at night, he nearly died of fright meeting a Jersey cow; Stanley answers with Earl Hines's funeral-home story.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: His father's heart trouble and death at 47
segments.summary: His father got short of breath driving, had heart trouble and died at 47, which was before McShann headed to Omaha.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Stopping in Kansas City, the Reno Club and Bill Hadnot
segments.summary: On a layover he walked into the Reno Club, where bassist Bill Hadnot, an old Tulsa friend, was playing with Bus Moten's band and gave him his room.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Monroe Inn with drummer Elmer Hopkins and Dave Dexter's write-up
segments.summary: He got a duo job with drummer Elmer Hopkins at the Monroe Inn, where Dave Dexter wrote them up in the Journal-Post.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: Walter Bales, the union and the two-piano rich man
segments.summary: A white millionaire and pianist, Walter Bales, read the write-up and sought McShann out through the union; he had played two pianos with Basie.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: The country club party, tips and giving away half-pints in a cab
segments.summary: At Bales's country club party he made big tips plus a $20 check and a basket of half-pints, and handed them out from a cab on 18th and 12th Streets.

segments.chapter: First big band, his father, arriving in Kansas City
segments.title: His 1937 marriage and his wife's reaction to his tips
segments.summary: He married late in 1937; his wife did not understand a musician's life until he emptied a pocketful of tips, about $65-70, on the table.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Taking the first group into the 2-10 Club
segments.summary: Bales got him a spot at Martin's plaza club, the start of the 2-10; the first group had Gates, Popeye, Bob Mabane, Gene Ramey and his cousin Pete McShann.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Changing the band: Hadnot, Gene Ramey and Countess Johnson
segments.summary: On Bales's advice he changed trumpet and drummer; Hadnot left for St. Louis, Gene Ramey joined from Countess Johnson's group, and McShann sizes up her playing.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Hearing Charlie Parker for the first time
segments.summary: He first heard Charlie Parker blowing at a club near the Monroe Inn after Bird's woodshedding in the Ozarks; Bird later went to New York and saw the Savoy.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Bird's first taste of the habit
segments.summary: He says he thinks Bird first got into drugs while in the small band, but that Bird apparently kicked it before joining Harlan Leonard.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Bird leaves Harlan Leonard to join the big band
segments.summary: After a battle of the bands with Harlan Leonard, Bird gave notice and joined McShann's big band, where he rehearsed the reed section.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Tadd Dameron and the phrasing difference from Harlan Leonard
segments.summary: Dameron wrote for Harlan Leonard; McShann explains his band phrased in long lines that 'sang' and agrees Andy Kirk's band lacked a lead man.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Lead alto duties, Bird's tone and Bird as a blues player
segments.summary: John Jackson phrased written parts and Bird the head tunes; McShann argues that Bird, despite a thin tone, was the greatest blues player.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Bird at his peak in the big band and the missing records
segments.summary: He thinks Bird played best with the big band, citing a long Cherokee at a Baltimore broadcast, and wishes he could have recorded more.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Founding the big band: Century Room, Bales's money, Tomino
segments.summary: Dexter urged him to keep the small band, but he took a Century Room job and enlarged it with Nat Towles men; Bales funded that, and the records paid for the rest.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Losing the value of money on the big band
segments.summary: He admits he was worse with money once he had a big band and refused to downsize after the Army.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Nights of listening in Kansas City: Pete Johnson and Joe Turner
segments.summary: When he first arrived he went to every club after work, hearing Bus Moten and Pete Johnson's steady beat behind Joe Turner on 12th Street.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Hearing Mary Lou Williams, Basie and other big bands
segments.summary: He first heard Mary Lou Williams with Andy Kirk at Fairyland Park and caught Basie's group when they returned; Ben Webster and Lester were gone.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Arrangers: Tadd Dameron and Willie Scott
segments.summary: Tadd Dameron and tenor man Willie Scott wrote for the band; Scott had played with Margaret Johnson's band and joined the army around 1940.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: How head arrangements set the band's style
segments.summary: Their style came from head arrangements built at rehearsal, with numbers lasting up to 30 minutes and a rhythm section building choruses before the horns entered.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: 'Sport Them Up' and riffs that never clashed
segments.summary: He explains how Willow Weep for Me was played as 'Sport Them Up' with different riffs from reeds, brass and trombones that never clashed.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Written arrangements adapted to the band's style
segments.summary: Stanley says some written arrangements were stiffer than the heads; McShann says the players made them sound like the band's own way.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: How long Bird stayed with the big band
segments.summary: McShann dates Bird's stay with the big band to about four years, from 1940 to late 1943, after which Bird lost interest.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Bird leaves for Earl Hines
segments.summary: Bird left in 1943 for Earl Hines after Andy Kirk took him to New York; Hines promised to straighten him out and soon begged McShann to take him back.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Bird's overdose in Detroit and the stocking feet
segments.summary: McShann let Bird go after he overdosed at the Paradise in Detroit and came on stage in stocking feet.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Playing Don Redman's booked dates when bookings ran short
segments.summary: When bookings fell short, the band played dates sold as Don Redman's, with Redman waving the baton while they played their own book.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Gene Ramey looks after Bird's lateness
segments.summary: Bird's timekeeping worsened and Gene Ramey took charge of getting him to jobs, though McShann says that was bad for other players.

segments.chapter: Small band, Charlie Parker and the big band
segments.title: Bird's reception in Kansas City versus the Savoy audience
segments.summary: He says Kansas City listeners liked Bird without needing to understand him, while at the Savoy the crowd ignored Bird's Body and Soul but cheered Jimmy Forrest.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Dancers and what bands teach them
segments.summary: They discuss whether Bird's music suited dancers and agree a band educates its dancers, who dance to what they grasp.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Bird could swing but Dizzy could not
segments.summary: He argues Bird swung while Dizzy was a technical player who never swung, and Stanley asks about Milt Jackson, interrupted by a recording glitch.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Dizzy's groups and drummers who could not swing the big band
segments.summary: He says Dizzy's groups did not swing like his sessions with Bird, citing Mickey Roker unable to swing a big band in Europe, and swinging is subjective.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Benny Bailey versus Art Farmer
segments.summary: He says Art Farmer could not swing like Benny Bailey, who played with his West Coast group; players fit different rhythm sections.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Latin rhythm, George Benson and the meaning of swing
segments.summary: They debate whether Latin rhythm sections swing; McShann says Latin is structural while swing is free, praising George Benson's flexibility.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Does the band swing every night, and why hungry bands play best
segments.summary: He says his band had to swing every night, and that bands play best when they come off the road hungry rather than after a big meal.

segments.chapter: Swing and what makes a band play
segments.title: Toothache and break in the interview
segments.summary: McShann's tooth bothers him and they agree to pause and take a pill before talking about the Savoy and Lucky Millinder.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Walter Brown and the first Decca session in Dallas
segments.summary: He found singer Walter Brown on 18th Street and in ten days rehearsed Hootie Blues and Confessing the Blues for the Decca session, where Dave Kapp wanted blues and boogie.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Getting Al Hibbler to join the band
segments.summary: The telegram and ticket to Hibbler were intercepted by his girlfriend; McShann finally reached him through a friend and brought him to Kansas City.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: The Cassadel in Tulsa expecting a white band
segments.summary: In Tulsa band members first heard Confessin' the Blues on a jukebox, and the club owner had expected a white band because of the McShann name.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Being pushed to play blues after the hit
segments.summary: The record's success forced them to play vocal blues behind Brown, though before it their blues were instrumental, and live versions ran five to six minutes.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: How he got the nickname Hootie
segments.summary: He explains his nickname Hootie came from getting sick on spiked beer at the Greenleaf Club, and that Jesse Price started it.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Moe Gale, Chicago, Gary and the Paradise Theatre in Detroit
segments.summary: Tim Gale heard the band at Gary, Indiana on the way east; their first theatre date at Detroit's Paradise was a hit, especially Hibbler and Walter Brown.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Arriving at the Savoy in 1941 with the Sultans
segments.summary: They opened at the Savoy Ballroom in 1941, after Chick Webb's death, playing a private party and then alongside the Sultans.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Battle with Lucky Millinder's band
segments.summary: McShann held back for three sets, then the band went into its books and out-played Lucky Millinder's, who afterwards fired three men.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: The secret of Roll 'Em
segments.summary: He says the secret of Kansas City Roll 'Em was the whole band, built from the rhythm section's chorus-by-chorus generator.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Ben Webster tells 52nd Street to go uptown to the Savoy
segments.summary: Ben Webster told saxophonists on 52nd Street to go to the Savoy to learn from the young Kansas City band, and funnily described them sneaking in.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Savoy stays, Gale bookings and Don Redman billing
segments.summary: The band alternated weeks in and out of the Savoy, was booked by Gale in theatres and nearby territory, and played Christmas dates billed as Redman's.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: The failed southern tour
segments.summary: On a southern tour booked by Gale there was no advertising at the venues, they ran short of money and had to ask New York for more.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: Gale demands repayment and Tomino heads for Chicago
segments.summary: The Gale office said it needed its money back or a share of the band, and Tomino left for Chicago while McShann was kept in New York.

segments.chapter: Decca records, the Savoy and Moe Gale
segments.title: GAC books 40 one-nighters and McShann pays off Gale
segments.summary: Berle Adams at GAC booked 40 one-nighters; McShann paid off Gale with a check in Cincinnati to Ben Bart, who had expected to take over.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Tape header for sides 5-6
segments.summary: Header for sides 5-6, Washington, D.C.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: GAC bookings, Clyde Bernhardt and 90 straight one-nighters
segments.summary: He went into the Army in May 1944 after GAC booked solidly; trombonist Clyde Bernhardt joined and complained that 90 straight one-nighters was too much.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Wartime travel and booking commissions
segments.summary: They travelled by bus and crowded troop trains; booking fees were 15 percent for one-nighters and ten for locations.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Taken off the bandstand for the draft at Kansas City
segments.summary: Booked a year ahead, he kept missing draft papers until two men arrived at the Kansas City auditorium and took him to Leavenworth.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: The band's music book stolen after he went in
segments.summary: Pianist George Salsbury finished the night; McShann told John Tomino to take the music home but it was stolen from the stand, so the band could not carry on.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: The union rules he must pay for missed dates
segments.summary: After the war the union made McShann pay four promoters for missed dates because Tomino had not informed them.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Induction into an anti-aircraft unit
segments.summary: He was put in anti-aircraft training, was refused Special Service because of his papers, and was released after almost a year.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Playing the officers' club to avoid bivouac
segments.summary: At Camp Stewart, Georgia, he never joined the band, playing the officers' club and slipping out of rough exercises.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Flat feet, the doctor's note and the bayonet
segments.summary: A doctor was astonished by his flat feet and gave him a note; when a corporal tried to tip his bed he came out with a bayonet.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: How he finally got out: furlough, hospital and discharge
segments.summary: A sudden 14-day furlough, a hemorrhoid operation and a review of his record led to discharge at the Sheraton near Chicago.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: After release: Capitol session with Julia Lee and a New York job
segments.summary: On his return to Kansas City, Dave Dexter had him back Julia Lee on a Capitol session before he took a 52nd Street job to rebuild the band.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Ending the postwar big band on the West Coast
segments.summary: He broke up the new big band in California after a Leeds publishing check, because he was losing money on every date.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Jimmy Witherspoon joins at Vallejo
segments.summary: When Blues Bailey left for Charlie Barnet, Jimmy Witherspoon sat in at a Vallejo dance and finished the dates.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: When he started singing himself
segments.summary: He did not sing until about 1968, when audiences demanded the old hits like Hootie Blues, and he took it up.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: The West Coast small group: Witherspoon, Benny Bailey, Art Farmer
segments.summary: Witherspoon praised his time with McShann; the small group had Floating Moody, Pete McShann and Addison Farmer, then Art Farmer replaced Benny Bailey.

segments.chapter: Army service and after the war
segments.title: Bootleg sessions and Ain't Nobody's Business
segments.summary: During the recording ban he cut sessions under Witherspoon's name, including Ain't Nobody's Business, a big hit that earned McShann only session pay.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Studio session work behind other singers on the West Coast
segments.summary: After the band folded he mostly recorded behind other artists for labels like Down Beat and Modern, at double pay, often uncredited.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: After-hours with Art Tatum, who could not be asked to play
segments.summary: He drove Art Tatum to after-hours spots until dawn; Tatum hated being asked to play and would sit down when ready.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Tatum needed no drummer and loved to play and sing the blues
segments.summary: He says Tatum needed no rhythm section and could throw drummers off, and that Tatum loved the blues and sometimes sang them.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Back to South Bend, Jesse Price and a southern tour of his own
segments.summary: Called home to South Bend by a sick child, he formed a group with Jesse Price and Ernie Shepherd and booked a southern tour himself via local promoters, ending in Wichita.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Priscilla Bowman, 'Hands Off' and the Johnny Baker's job in Kansas City
segments.summary: He moved to Kansas City in 1951 and played about five years at Johnny Baker's with a sextet, interrupted by the 1955 Priscilla Bowman hit 'Hands Off'.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Priscilla Bowman and the Delta Queen riverboat trip
segments.summary: Bowman sang with him on a two-week Delta Queen trip up the Mississippi from New Orleans to Cincinnati, sponsored by the University of Nebraska.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: First trip to Europe in 1969 and the T-Bone Walker session in Paris
segments.summary: His first European trip was in 1969 with Eddie Cleanhead Vincent, Gene Ramey and Paul Gunther; in Paris he recalls recording with a sick, heavy-drinking T-Bone Walker in Paris, with Hal Singer, whom he told not to argue with him.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Popularity in Europe and the Michael's Pub band
segments.summary: He has toured Europe every year since, finds himself more popular there, and lists the band he used at Michael's Pub.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Jay McShann Day, the keys to the city and Claude Williams
segments.summary: In 1978 Kansas City gave him the keys to the city at the Muhlbach with an all-star band; he first worked with Claude Williams about 1969.

segments.chapter: Postwar career: studio work, Kansas City, Europe
segments.title: Why Kansas City has so little jazz now
segments.summary: They note that visitors ask where Kansas City's jazz is, and McShann says there is little, though the Muhlbach has begun booking groups.

segments.chapter: School, honors and the film
segments.title: Studying at the Kansas City Conservatory
segments.summary: With his kids in school he enrolled at the Conservatory to learn harmony, composition, ear training and to read, wanting to know what he was doing.

segments.chapter: School, honors and the film
segments.title: Dr. Boubendorf, the strict German teacher who asked him to play
segments.summary: His strict German teacher Dr. Boubendorf corrected his habits, then heard him playing his own pieces and had him play for the class.

segments.chapter: School, honors and the film
segments.title: The film The Last of the Blue Devils and closing thanks
segments.summary: He describes Bruce Ricker's Kansas City jazz film, shot at the Musicians Foundation, which ran short of money; the interview ends with thanks.
